events.title: Boeing chosen by U.S. navy to develop next-generation fighter jet
events.summary: The U.S. Navy said Tuesday it awarded Boeing a contract to develop its next-generation fighter jets. The contract is worth more than $20 billion for the full-scale development phase. Boeing was also tapped by the Air Force to develop its F-47 fighter in 2025. Aircraft manufacturer Boeing has been selected by the Pentagon and U.S. Navy to develop the next generation of fighter jets. The contract, worth more than $20 billion, is to build its Sixth-Generation F/A-XX Strike Fighter over a long-term phase, the defense departments said . The F/A-XX is intended to replace the service's fleet of F/A-18 Super Hornets. The fighter will advance open mission systems architecture, advanced mission systems, and operational reach and capacity, Boeing said in a separate statement. The stock closed 1.8% higher at the end of the trading day on Tuesday. "The F/A-XX is a critical pillar in our commitment to maintaining peace through strength. F/A-XX will dominate contested airspace, extend operational reach, and deliver a decisive combat advantage for the warfighter," said Michael P. Duffey, Under Secretary of War for acquisition and sustainment. It marks the company's second prestigious sixth-generation jet contract in a year after the Air Force selected it to develop its F-47 fighter in 2025. Elsewhere, Boeing recently flagged a software glitch in some of its 737 Max 10 aircraft that could impact certain landing procedures, which led the Federal Aviation Administration on Monday to delay its certification of the aircraft. "We haven't concluded whether this is a safety-of-flight issue or not, but we will be delaying the 10 ... until we're satisfied that we don't have an issue here," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference on air traffic modernization in Washington, D.C., on Monday.

events.title: How Hong Kong entices Europe’s young start-up talent
events.summary: Winner of Hong Kong Talent Engage-backed hackathon shares insights after a visit to southern China’s innovation and technology hubs Hong Kong’s efforts in advancing the city’s innovation and technology (I&T) industry have been highlighted in a number of international surveys in recent years. One of the most recent was the International Institute for Management Development’s “World Competitiveness Ranking 2026”, which placed Hong Kong second among 70 economies worldwide. The city is also part of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou innovation cluster, which retained first place globally in the World Intellectual Property Organization’s “Global Innovation Index 2026”. It ranked regions on the basis of how many inventors, scientific authors and venture capitalists they had after analysing their patent filings, scientific publications and start-up funding deals. In addition to Hong Kong’s existing advantages for start-ups – which include its proximity to the manufacturing hubs in Southern China’s Greater Bay Area development zone and the government-backed funding schemes for research and development – it can also offer a stable supply of high-calibre talent with diverse I&T backgrounds and experience. Unsurprisingly, Hong Kong’s start-up ecosystem has expanded – up from over 1,500 start-ups in 2015 to more than 5,200 last year, according to the latest government data. Hong Kong Talent Engage (HKTE), an office under the Labour and Welfare Bureau, has been working tirelessly to promote the city’s advantages and schemes to attract talented technology professionals from around the world since it was established in 2023. One of its latest efforts included co-hosting the HKTE x EuroTech Hackathon in Munich, Germany in June. About 250 contestants from universities and start-ups across Europe took part in the competition, which saw them asked to devise ideas and concepts that addressed practical challenges relevant to Hong Kong. Earlier this month, HKTE invited the winners of the hackathon and representatives from the EuroTech Federation as part of a 20-member delegation to visit Hong Kong and its neighbouring cities to gain first-hand experience of the region’s rapidly developing I&T infrastructure. One of them was Cem Araz, whose team won the hackathon’s healthtech category. Araz is the CEO and co-founder of Munich-based start-up firm Heal, which runs Heal Health, a preventive-health app that offers blood-test results and data and AI-led guidance, including personalised recommendations and follow-up actions, to users’ wearable devices. His team’s hackathon-winning concept, an AI-powered eyelid scanner intended to identify possible low haemoglobin levels from photographs, complements Heal’s broader focus on helping people understand health data earlier and act on it. Although Heal’s immediate focus remains on Europe, the visit reinforced Araz’s interest in taking the start-up to Hong Kong or another city within the bay area scheme in the future. He believes Hong Kong offers the right investment opportunities, start-up support and regulatory environment to serve as a potential base for building an AI-enabled preventive-health business, and says the region’s demographic needs could create a relevant opportunity for preventive health technology. “Heal’s concept could be a valuable idea to bring to Hong Kong because the city has an ageing population,” he says. “I believe that would be a win-win for both sides.” The five-day programme offered Araz and the other hackathon winners a close-up view of the I&T ecosystems taking shape across Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou. The group toured key I&T hubs in the region. They included Hong Kong Science Park in Pak Shek Kok, Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park at the Lok Ma Chau Loop, Cyberport in Pok Fu Lam and Northern Metropolis in the northern New Territories, a strategic development area focused on research, I&T and cross-border collaboration between Hong Kong and the mainland. In Qianhai in Shenzhen and Nansha in Guangzhou, they also visited I&T organisations and enterprises specialising in industrial applications in AI, robotics, smart transport and biotechnology. Araz says one of the most useful parts of the trip was the opportunity to talk to entrepreneurs already based in Hong Kong. He was also impressed by the scale and range of technology applications on display in Shenzhen, including the autonomous-driving demonstrations and drone food delivery, which are not yet common in Germany. He was particularly excited to see the innovations on show at technology and entertainment conglomerate Tencent Holdings. “As the founder of a young, early-stage start-up, to see such success is a big inspiration,” he says. “The whole trip was a learning [experience] for me – to see how people work and how engaged and innovative they are.

events.title: Temasek to expand in the Middle East, plans to open offices in Riyadh and Abu Dhabi
events.summary: Temasek says it sees significant long-term opportunities in the Middle East for itself and its portfolio companies. Temasek plans to expand in the Middle East by opening offices in Riyadh and Abu Dhabi by mid-2027, aiming to create strategic hubs and deepen regional partnerships. The company sees significant long-term opportunities due to the region's economic transformation and diversification, aligning with Temasek's investment focus and expertise. Temasek's expansion will boost access to broader Central Asia and Africa markets, enhancing its global network with 15 offices across 11 countries by 2027 for sustainable long-term returns. SINGAPORE – Despite the ongoing conflict in the Middle East , Singapore’s global investment company Temasek plans to expand its presence in the region. This includes opening offices in Riyadh in Saudi Arabia, and Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates by the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. These offices will also serve as strategic hubs where some portfolio companies can be co-located. Temasek will also actively engage institutions in Qatar and other markets in the Middle East, to pursue partnership and investment opportunities, it said in a statement on Sept 30. It sees “significant long-term opportunities for itself and its portfolio companies” in the Middle East, where its strategic expansion will also strengthens its ability to access opportunities across broader Central Asia and Africa. “The region is undergoing a broad-based economic transformation, driven by ambitious national development and diversification plans,” it said. “Temasek’s global investment experience, networks, and partnership-led approach, alongside its portfolio companies’ deep domain expertise, can contribute to the region’s growth.” Temasek Holdings chief executive Dilhan Pillay Sandrasegara said: “The Middle East is an important part of Temasek’s global network. “The pace and ambition of economic transformation across the region are remarkable, and its long-term fundamentals remain highly attractive.” He added that Temasek sees strong alignment between the region’s priorities and Temasek’s own areas of focus. “Our relationships across the Middle East – particularly in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar – have been built over many years through our partnerships, co-investments, and portfolio companies, and we look forward to deepening them further. “This expansion is a natural next step, and it will help us create compelling partnerships to grow together,” he said. Temasek Global Investments chief executive officer Chia Song Hwee said being on the ground in the Middle East will also “allows us to bring complementary expertise from across our ecosystem to these markets, expanding pathways to create lasting value with like-minded partners”. Chia was appointed chairman of the Middle East and Africa region with effect from Sept 1. In this role, he will provide senior leadership and oversight of Temasek’s engagement and long-term growth in these markets. Ankit Khemka is managing director of the region and will also continue to drive Temasek’s strategy and expansion there. In July, Temasek said that around 12 % of its portfolio is exposed to the Europe, Middle East and Africa region , with most of it in Europe. At the time, Chia said Temasek began looking more deeply into the Middle East market over the past two to three years, starting with fund investments. With the two new offices, Temasek will have 15 offices across 11 countries in 2027. This network strengthens its ability to operate as a global investor with deep regional connectivity, built to deliver good sustainable returns over the long term, Temasek said. Besides the Middle East, Temasek has offices across nine countries: Beijing, Hanoi, Mumbai, Shanghai, Shenzhen, and Singapore in Asia; and Brussels, London, Mexico City, New York, Paris, San Francisco, and Washington, DC outside Asia. Sue-Ann Tan is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, covering capital markets and sustainable finance.

events.title: Poundland management in rescue talks that could save 11,000 jobs
events.summary: Ex-Asda boss Andy Bond linked to plan, with buyout team understood to be negotiating with financial backer Poundland’s management team are in “advanced talks” to lead a rescue bid for the ailing cut-price retailer that could save more than 11,000 jobs. The former Asda boss Andy Bond, who ran Poundland for a number of years from 2016 then stepped up to its former parent Pepco before leaving in 2025, is understood to be part of the negotiations to take on the business. The management buyout team, which includes the current boss Barry Williams, are understood to be negotiating with an unnamed financial backer. Poundland’s current owners, Gordon Brothers, last month hired the advisory company Alvarez & Marsal to oversee a sale of the business at a reported price of £30m. The process has fuelled fears that the restructuring specialist is set on breaking up the retailer despite improved trading. Interested parties are thought to include the US company Fortress, which owns Poundstretcher, and Modella Capital, the UK-based private equity owner of Hobbycraft and TG Jones that this year put the UK arm of Claire’s Accessories and The Original Factory Shop into administration . Neither of these players are involved with Bond’s team. Sources said these financial companies were among those placing a first round of bids at the start of this week that are to be considered as early as Wednesday. One source said very few bids were expected to include the entire business and it was a “great shame” if an offer to keep the business trading was not considered. The discount chain, which employs 11,000 people and has 600 stores, said last week that it had returned to growth of 3.3% at established stores in the latest three-month period. “Profitability is on a strongly improving trajectory with expected pre-tax earnings around £80m better than last year.” The company registered an £85m pre-tax loss in the year to the end of September 2025 but said it had a cash pile of more than £30m and several sources of borrowings. Gordon Brothers had put in place a £95m lending facility, of which only £50m had been used, Poundland said. The restructuring specialist, which bought Poundland from for £1 from Pepco Group in June 2025, agreed to pump £80m into the company as part of a rescue deal last year. events.title: The 5 most surprising takeaways from Sam Altman at OpenAI's big developer conference
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaks at the company's DevDay conference on Tuesday. Bloomberg/Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is the face of the AI boom. Here's what he said at his flagship conference. Tokens are "terrible," and the "Industrial Revolution" is a bad way to understand AI, Altman said. When it comes to AI safety, Altman said the tech industry should take a "centrist path." If OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stands at the center of the AI boom, what he says about the technology can blaze a trail for the rest of the industry. At OpenAI's DevDay conference on Tuesday in San Francisco, Altman announced the launch of a new AI agent product called Dots and laid out the company's grand ambitions . He also set out some of his ideals, quibbled with how AI is understood, and talked about how OpenAI's new product is changing his morning routine. Of course, everything Altman says should be viewed through a certain frame — he owes financial success to his investors , is competing with Anthropic and other AI companies, and wants to be seen as a capable steward of the powerful tech. Here are some of the most surprising points he made on Tuesday. Altman said AI shouldn't only 'turn the economic crank' President Donald Trump loves to refer to AI as an "Industrial Revolution," only bigger. Altman is not so much a fan of the term. Altman said he believes AI will have a greater impact on the world than the Industrial Revolution — a dramatic claim, given that it was one of the defining transitions in human history. He said that AI should focus more on empowering people. "I don't think the purpose of this technology is to just sort of like, turn the economic crank faster and faster for the sake of AIs," Altman said. "I think we should learn from the mistakes of the Industrial Revolution," he added, "and I think we should be more like the Renaissance." Altman said tokens are a 'terrible' measure of AI A token is a cluster of letters and the basic unit of AI's input and output. Companies like OpenAI use tokens to price their models, and corporate customers have grown accustomed to paying for AI access this way. Some developers have even been tokenmaxxing — using as many tokens as possible to appear more productive at work. Altman said Tuesday that tokens are a "terrible metric for a bunch of reasons," including that different models can churn through different numbers of tokens to complete the same task. In other words, they aren't a good proxy for the actual value of a task, in his view. The CEO said that his team has considered eliminating tokens entirely as a metric, though customers pushed back. They want some kind of "underlying basis" for what they pay, Altman said, and for now, tokens are it. "We have not figured out a better way to do that," he said. OpenAI's Dots help Altman escape brainrot OpenAI is building a device, and Altman said on Tuesday it would be "reasonable to assume" that the company's new personal AI agent tool, Dots , would run inside it. For now, the agent helps him get less attached to his smartphone, he said. Because it handles some tasks for him and processes his notifications, he feels calmer about his to-do list when he wakes up. "I feel like I've finally gotten some of my attention back," Altman said. "I no longer feel quite addicted to my phone in the same way." He later said that going through everything from overnight in the morning would make his "brain feel polluted, and now my Dot just deals with the stuff." Altman is figuring out his lane in AI safety Altman faced several questions about AI safety in the press Q&A, amid an ongoing surge in anxiety over newly capable AI models and a rise in cyber incidents. OpenAI has previously disclosed incidents where its AI agents have gone rogue . Altman framed the ongoing debate as flawed on either side. On one side, he said, are people who want to charge ahead in the industry and keep quickly ramping up AI's capabilities — basically, the people who downplay safety concerns. On the other hand, many people think AI development should be fully paused or shut down. Altman said he can imagine things going wrong in either direction: loss-of-control incidents amid an AI capability push, or a concentration of power if AI development stops. He said safety needs to stay ahead of capabilities, and the push forward should continue. "I think as an industry, we need to navigate this centrist path," Altman said. Altman says it's the 'best time' to enter the job market Concerns about the job market are top of mind for young people graduating into the midst of the AI boom. The unemployment rate for recent college graduates in the US was 5.7% in June, according to the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, In response to a young attendee's ask for advice on Tuesday, Altman said, "I think this is the best time to be entering the job market, except hopefully all the time in the future." He said that gloom-and-doom predictions about job loss largely underestimate how much the economy will grow. The argument stands in stark contrast with what Altman previously said . "There will be some classes of jobs that will totally go away, but if you are an ambitious person graduating college right now, I think it's probably the best time thus far in history," Altman said. events.title: UK economy ‘slightly larger’ than previously thought after Q2 growth revised up; Greggs proposes 740 job cuts – business live
events.summary: Introduction: UK economy bigger than first thought after GDP revised higher Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy. The UK economy grew faster than first estimated in the second quarter of the year, despite the disruption caused by the Iran war. UK growth in April-June has been revised to 0.5%, up from the previous estimate of 0.4%, in the latest National Accounts. That’s a welcome piece of good news for chancellor John Healey, as he draws up the budget due in four weeks’ time, and means his predecessor Rachel Reeves handed over a slightly larger economy than previously recognised. Growth in Q2 2026 was driven by the services sector (where activity increased by 0.6%) and the construction sector (which grew by 0.8%), while the production sector shrank by 0.1%. However…the Office for National Statistics , which publishes the data, has also revised down its estimate for growth in 2025. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said: “Today’s figures include our annual improvements to the measurement of the economy, incorporating new information that provides a better picture of activity across the UK’s service sector, alongside the usual inclusion of updated and improved data sources. “Growth for 2025 as a whole was a little lower than previously estimated, with the profile of growth across the quarters also revised. “However, stronger services growth in the latest quarter means the economy is now slightly larger than previously estimated.” 7am BST: UK national accounts for April-June 2026 7.45am BST: French inflation report for September 10:30am BST: BoE Financial Policy Committee minutes 1.30pm BST: US PCE inflation index for August 19m ago Zoopla: House sales down 9% in September 43m ago GDP upgrade is 'boost to Burnham' but winter slowdown looms 1h ago UK cements position as fastest-growing G7 country this year 1h ago Greggs proposes 740 job cuts 2h ago Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January 2h ago UK business investment jumps as 'AI-driven wave' arrives 2h ago UK living standards picked up in April-June 2h ago Introduction: UK economy bigger than first thought after GDP revised higher Zoopla: House sales down 9% in September Higher borrowing costs hurt demand for homes in September, the property portal Zoopla has reported this morning. Zoopla found that the number of sales being agreed this month fell by 9% compared with September 2025. The drop in sales came despite the number of homes on the market rising by 5% year on year, with the gap between supply and demand most acute in London and southern England. Annual house price growth has also slowed to 0.8%, the lowest level since July 2024, according to the latest Zoopla House Price Index. The average price of a UK home is now £273,000, it said. GDP upgrade is 'boost to Burnham' but winter slowdown looms This morning’s upgrade to UK growth in April-June is a boost to Andy Burnham, analysts say, even though he didn’t take office until almost a month later. Chris Beauchamp , chief market analyst at IG , says: “Still on a post-speech high, the upgraded figure is yet more good news for the UK’s still-new(ish) prime minister. The highest growth in the G7 for the first half is certainly a headline and one that will help keep nervous MPs in line for a while, plus it helps take off pressure for a new election - why risk it now when things appear to be improving nicely.” Ashley Webb , senior UK economist at Capital Economics , warns though that growth may slow towards the end of this year: The upward revision to real GDP growth in Q2, from 0.4% q/q to 0.5% q/q, suggests that the economy has been a bit more resilient to higher energy prices in the first half of the year than previously thought. This resilience may continue into Q3, but we still expect it to fade in Q4 as higher inflation takes a bigger bite out of households’ real incomes. The 0.5% q/q gain in Q2 real GDP followed unrevised growth of 0.6% q/q in Q1, with the breakdown still showing that the economy is no longer being heavily supported by government spending, which contracted by 0.5% q/q (revised down from -0.3%). Thomas Pugh, chief economist at audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK, agrees that growth will slow over the winter: “The upward revisions to Q2 GDP growth means the economy was even stronger in the first half of the year than we previously expected, despite the Iran war. What’s more, the composition of growth looks a little healthier. Surveys suggest that much of that positive momentum has been carried forward into Q3 meaning we have revised up our annual GDP forecast to 1.4%. “However, the next six months looks tougher with potential interest rate rises, a sharp increase in inflation and another tax raising budget all to come. That will drag heavily on growth over the winter. Investors are cheered that Greggs now expects “a modestly improved outcome for 2026”.

events.title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief; Qatar pushes for peace talks
events.summary: President Donald Trump has denied offering Iran sanctions relief. Qatar continued to mediate between Washington and Tehran, with Iran's foreign minister due to report on U.S. feedback on proposals to unlock the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. President Donald Trump has denied reports that he had offered sanctions relief to Iran in exchange for concessions from Tehran on its nuclear program. The president in a Truth Social post dismissed an Axios report that indicated he was willing to give Tehran sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in return for "concrete steps" on its nuclear program. "This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING!," Trump wrote, dismissing the Axios story, as a "HOAX." Brent crude , the international price benchmark, was was down 0.31% at $102.27 per barrel at 3:36 a.m. E.T., reversing earlier gains. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were down 0.47% at $88.96 a barrel. The increase in oil prices comes as Qatar continues its push to broker a lasting peace settlement between Washington and Tehran. Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araqchi met with Qatari mediators in Doha late Tuesday, where he received U.S. feedback on the Islamic Republic's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Araqchi will discuss the response in Tehran on Wednesday. Qatari foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said the country continues to exchange messages between the two parties. "We're working towards establishing a common ground in order to get into a deal that would save all of us from the repercussions of the conflict," he told reporters.

events.title: Banks raise interest rates after RBA lifts cash rate to highest since 2011
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Major banks raise interest rates after RBA lifts cash rate to highest since 2011 All of the big four banks have passed on the latest RBA rate hike in full. ( ABC News: Alistair Kroie ) Australia's major banks will lift variable home loan rates by 0.25 per cent from next month, after the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) lifted the cash rate to its highest level in more than a decade. The Reserve Bank increases interest rates to 4.6 per cent in its fourth rate rise this year. This week's RBA decision took the country's cash rate to 4.6 per cent, an increase of 0.25 per cent, and the fourth hike this year. The cash rate is the highest it has been since November 2011. Commonwealth Bank, NAB, Westpac and ANZ announced increases to home loan variable interest rates by 0.25 per cent per annum, effective October 9. CBA's group executive retail banking, Angus Sullivan, said the RBA's decision came during persistent inflation and ongoing global uncertainty, which were adding to economic pressures. Most banks acknowledged many mortgage holders may struggle with the increased payments. NAB group executive personal banking, Ana Marinkovic, said concerned customers should contact the bank early about their finances. Westpac chief executive, consumer, Carolyn McCann, acknowledged the increase would impact households' cost-of-living pressures. What's impacted in the RBA rate hike While the RBA's decisions are most felt through mortgage repayments, their impact extends well beyond home loans. ANZ said it was reviewing its other interest rates. Macquarie Bank also announced it would make changes to interest rates across its variable home loan and deposit products from October 15. Its variable interest rates on transaction and savings accounts will increase by 0.25 per cent per annum, along with its variable home loan reference rates. events.title: Asia’s top tech start-ups move beyond software towards physical AI
events.summary: Granite Asia said the cohort of 2026 stands out for how far it has moved beyond enterprise software. Asia’s top tech start-ups are expanding AI use beyond software into physical applications like wind farms, warehouses, and healthcare. The 2026 NextGen Tech 30 list features over half of companies focused on these advanced AI solutions. The initiative by Granite Asia and SGX aims to support these growth-stage firms to scale globally from Asia. SINGAPORE – Asia’s growth-stage technology companies are increasingly taking artificial intelligence beyond software and into the physical world, deploying it across wind farms, warehouses, construction sites, operating theatres and even low-Earth orbit. More than half of the 30 companies named in the 2026 NextGen Tech 30 (NGT30), a list of Asia’s top 30 growth-stage technology companies by Singapore-headquartered investment platform Granite Asia released on Sept 30, reflect this shift. Now in its third year, NGT30 is Asia’s first public-private initiative to recognise and support the region’s top growth-stage technology companies. Run by Granite Asia in partnership with the Singapore Exchange (SGX), the programme brings together sovereign wealth funds, institutional investors, government agencies and industry leaders to support companies with the potential to scale globally from Asia. Granite Asia said the cohor t of 2026 stands out for how far it has moved beyond enterprise software. “Three years ago, a lot of software companies were building software to try and change the world,” said Jenny Lee, venture capitalist and senior managing partner at Granite Asia. “This year, we have companies creating robots to repair wind turbines, doing underwater vessel repair and using AI models to screen for cancer.” Lee was speaking at the NGT30 event at the SGX IPO Arena on the morning of Sept 30 , where the honourees were announced. Chee Hong Tat, minister for national development and deputy chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said the 30 companies recognised in 2026 reflected the growing depth and breadth of Asia’s innovation base. events.title: ‘Dire situation’: Lebanese prisoners on hunger strike for 18 days
events.summary: The medical condition of dozens of prisoners has deteriorated as inmates protest against suspension of amnesty law. The medical condition of dozens of inmates on a hunger strike for more than two weeks inside Lebanon’s largest prison has become “dire”, according to a legal campaigner. “About 400 prisoners are on a hunger strike for more than two weeks. Ambulances enter daily to take [dozens of] them away because their condition is dire,” Mohammed Sablouh, a Lebanese lawyer, told Al Jazeera. list 1 of 3 Syria and Lebanon make ‘significant progress’ at talks on joint interests list 2 of 3 Lebanon and Syria reshape ties amid Israeli attacks and regional shifts list 3 of 3 Lebanon passes long-sought amnesty law, a day after death penalty repeal “The prisoners are refusing medication, food and water,” Sablouh, who is also the director of the Prisoners’ Rights Center at the Tripoli Bar Association, said on Wednesday. The inmates at Roumieh prison went on a hunger strike on September 12 in protest against the suspension of a general amnesty law, which could have granted an immediate release or reduced their sentences. Protests have also been staged in Lebanon’s second city of Tripoli against the suspension of the law, which has a provision to release inmates jailed for petty crimes. Many of the prisoners on hunger strike were arrested for their solidarity with the Syrian revolution against President Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled in December 2024 after more than 10 years of bloody war. The Free Patriotic Movement, one of the country’s largest parties, filed an appeal before the Constitutional Council over concerns that some of the inmates were charged with “terrorism”. The Constitutional Council is expected to issue its verdict next month. Lebanese prisons are notorious for being overcrowded and thousands of inmates spend years behind bars without trial. Lebanon’s current prison population stands at about 8,500, nearly double its capacity. The law passed on August 12 aimed to address overcrowded prison conditions in the country. “Prison overcrowding exceeds 330 percent of the facilities’ actual capacity,” Sablouh said. “The situation in Lebanon’s prisons is truly tragic, it can no longer withstand any … shock or any overturning of the amnesty law.” More than 40 prisoners died in 2025. “Some died due to medical neglect, others under torture. Some died by suicide due to prolonged trials and repeated postponements,” Sablouh said. The Lebanese lawyer blamed judicial delays for the large number of inmates, many of them arrested for petty crimes. He pointed out the failure of the judiciary “to adhere to Article 108 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which sets a limit for pre-trial detention: two months for misdemeanours, renewable for an equal period, and six months for felonies, renewable for an equal period [up to a maximum of one year].”

events.title: People troll my DIY but they just spur me on
events.summary: Jasmine Gurney says her DIY social media posts took off during Covid lockdowns Published 30 September 2026, 00:06 BST It's hard to miss the explosion of DIY content that has hit our social media feeds over the last decade. From quick reels on how to fix cracks in walls, to complicated YouTube tutorials on building alcove seating from scratch, the internet is chock-a-block with seemingly endless home improvement demos. While DIY was once seen as more of a male domain, female influencers are inspiring a new generation of women to take matters into their own hands. Meanwhile, demand for female professionals is rising, while some women are changing careers to take up trades which they see as more AI-proof than their desk jobs. Eight months pregnant and building wardrobes DIY influencer Jasmine Gurney has documented an impressive and exhausting sounding list of tasks on Instagram. She has torn down partition walls, replaced flooring, erected a fence, insulated and boarded her loft, built an outdoor workshop, made custom cabinetry, moved plug sockets, made her son his first bed and has been building him a treehouse. Eight months pregnant, the former marketer is now racing to finish building a fitted wardrobe before the new baby arrives. "I like proving people wrong," says Jasmine, 33, from Bedfordshire, who says she's been trolled by people questioning her techniques but they just "spur me on more". "I'm showing and empowering other women to do it," she says. "I've shown me doing things whilst pregnant, I've had my firstborn strapped to me in a baby carrier while doing things. "I'm just showing that we are capable, we are interested in this sort of stuff and... we're sick of waiting around for six months for our husbands to pick up the tools and do it in most cases." Jasmine hopes she can inspire other women to give a project a go Jasmine says her page really took off during Covid when people couldn't get professionals in so needed to learn to do jobs themselves. While the lockdowns are long over, demand for content like hers has stuck, she believes, because there aren't enough tradespeople to meet demand, and cost of living pressures are squeezing budgets. Gen Z women are "leading the charge in challenging gendered DIY stereotypes", according to a 2024 report by B&Q. Around three-quarters of Gen Z women surveyed said they enjoy DIY, compared to 60% of all female respondents. And 82% of Gen Z women said seeing women doing more complex home DIY on social media had inspired them to do more themselves, versus 60% of women in general. Of course, not all jobs are DIY. Sometimes you'll need to GSI (get someone in). Bliss, 28, loves the freedom and flexibility of running a plumbing business Bliss Cunneen walked away from an Anthropology university course in 2020 to train as a plumber. The 28-year-old from south London says trying the trade on a whim is the "best thing I've ever done", and she loves the freedom and flexibility of running a business. While she has experienced doubt from some customers when she turns up at their door - and has even once been mistaken for the receptionist - "once you start working and you show you're confident and you know what you're doing, they're okay". She says the explosion of content online has "definitely helped" with broadening attitudes to women taking up DIY or a trade. TaskHer was set up to help people book tradeswomen Anna Moynihan set up TaskHer, a platform connecting female tradies with customers who need jobs done, after feeling frustrated when tradesmen she had booked for renovation work would address her husband rather than her. Five years ago she says she couldn't find any stock photographs of tradeswomen to use for marketing. Even the word "tradeswoman" would get autocorrected to "tradesman". "It's those little things that, you know, ultimately you don't feel welcome into that environment. "It's already hard enough to become a tradeswoman, a woman in an industry where you're massively under-represented." Enquiries on the site have more than doubled so far this year compared to 2025, while the number of tradeswomen signing up has almost quadrupled, Anna says. People might prefer a tradeswoman for a range of reasons - industry surveys suggest they may feel more at ease with a woman entering their home , external , feel a woman would be more respectful, or want to support women working in traditionally male roles. Anna Moynihan says some women are taking up a trade as they want the flexibility of working for themselves Anecdotally, Anna says more women are joining her platform after leaving white-collar jobs, adding three Oxford University-educated tradeswomen have signed up in the last month. She says some had always wanted to take up a trade but felt unable to up until now because of their gender. Others, she says, want the flexibility of working for themselves in a role less likely to be directly impacted by the rapid advance of AI.

events.summary: The Gambia come back to beat ‌Ghana 4-2, while Guinea Bissau beat Nigeria 3-0 despite seven Premier League starters. West ⁠African giants Ghana and Nigeria both suffered chastening defeats in Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers late Tuesday, while Algeria fought back from two goals down to avoid a shock loss to Burundi. Tiny Cape Verde, who won legions of admirers with their gutsy exploits at this year’s World Cup, also went down in a surprise home loss to Rwanda. list 1 of 4 Man City guilty of all serious financial breach charges: Premier League list 2 of 4 Ireland undecided on approach for next game against Israel, coach says list 3 of 4 Man City’s Premier League charges: What’s the latest and what comes next? list 4 of 4 ‘The emperor is naked’: UEFA’s Ceferin takes aim at FIFA boss Infantino But heavyweight contenders Egypt, Morocco and Senegal all won difficult away assignments, and there were home wins for Benin, Comoros, Gabon, the Ivory Coast, Mali, Mozambique, Uganda and Zambia on a busy day of 17 matches in the preliminaries for the 2027 finals to be cohosted by Kenya, Tanzania and ⁠Uganda. Ghana, one of Africa’s 10 representatives at the World Cup where they reached the last 32, surrendered a 2-0 lead in a stunning 4-2 home defeat by The Gambia in Accra. The Gambia, whose population is less than three million compared with Ghana’s almost 35 million, hit back through a Muhammed Badamosi penalty and goals from Omar Colley and substitute Ebrima Colley, who struck twice. Ernest Nuamah and Felix Afena-Gyan had put the Black Stars two goals ahead after 33 minutes, but their collapse prompted angry home supporters to throw bottles onto the pitch in the closing stages. The result ‌increased the pressure on veteran coach Carlos Queiroz after they opened their Group C campaign with a loss away to Ivory Coast last week. Coventry City’s Yann Gboho made a dramatic debut for Ivory Coast, coming off the bench to break Somalia’s stubborn resistance in the final minute before Bazoumana Toure added a second five minutes into stoppage time to complete a 2-0 win. Nigeria, who were semifinalists at the last Cup of Nations finals in January, had seven Premier League players in their starting lineup but were comprehensively outplayed as they went down 3-0 in Guinea Bissau, where the margin of defeat might have been even bigger. Franculino Dju curled home the first-half opener and captain Mama Balde made it 2-0 in the 66th minute. Alvaro Djalo added a third in stoppage time. Algeria fight back in their AFCON qualifier Algeria found themselves 2-0 down away in Burundi after 12 ⁠minutes but fought back to share the spoils in their Group I tie in Bujumbura. But it was a far from convincing performance ⁠under new coach Brahim Hemdani as Mohamed Belloumi and Adil Boulbina spared Algerian blushes. Cape Verde have now lost their opening two Group K clashes after Rwanda came from one goal down to win 2-1 in Praia with teenager Elie Iradukunda netting the decisive goal. In the same group, Mali won 1-0 away in Liberia. Egypt, who left Mohamed Salah at home over fears of potential injury on the artificial surface at Juba ⁠in South Sudan, ran out 5-0 winners with Omar Marmoush grabbing a double and Mostafa Zico, Ibrahim Adel, and teenager Hamza Abdelkarim also on target in the Group B clash. Brahim Diaz took advantage of sloppy defending to give Morocco the lead on the stroke of ⁠halftime away against Lesotho. The match was played in Bloemfontein, South Africa, because Lesotho does not have a stadium ⁠up to international standards. Azzedine Ounahi added a second eight minutes from time to complete the 2-0 victory that put Morocco top of Group A. Vieira secures first victory as Senegal coach Senegal had to defend tenaciously away against Ethiopia to give new coach Patrick Vieira his first win in charge after last week’s draw in Mozambique. Ibrahim Mbaye scored the game’s only goal after 11 minutes, having been teed up by a pass from his Aston Villa ‌teammate Nicolas Jackson. Mozambique went top of Group J on goal difference after demolishing Sudan 4-1 in Maputo with a double from striker Chamito, who plays his club football in Portugal’s third tier. Cameroon fought back for a 1-1 draw against Congo in Brazzaville while in the other Group G match, Comoros had a 1-0 home win in Moroni over Namibia, where ‌Benjaloud ‌Youssef scored early in the second half. The 2012 African champions Zambia beat Togo 2-0 in Ndola in a match halted for 20 minutes by a first-half power failure. Rodolfo Aloko scored both goals for Benin in their 2-1 win over Mauritania and debutant Arnold Vula netted Uganda’s goal in a 1-0 home triumph over Libya.

events.title: MAS proposes tighter board rules for S’pore banks, insurers
events.summary: The proposed updates build on revisions made in November 2021 to MAS’ guidelines on corporate governance for banks and insurers, as well as their designated financial holding companies. SINGAPORE – Banks and insurers incorporated here could soon see stricter corporate governance requirements such as an increased minimum board size and a majority of independent directors on the boards. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) is seeking feedback on proposed updates to corporate governance regulations for financial institutions (FIs) as part of its regular review of regulatory standards to keep them current and effective. “Strong corporate governance remains fundamental to well-run and resilient FIs. Banks and insurers play particularly critical roles in safeguarding depositor and policyholder interests. They perform important functions in supporting households, businesses and the wider economy,” MAS said on Sept 29. Updates have been proposed in four main areas: director independence, board composition, key appointments, and streamlining requirements for lower-impact FIs. Noting that “clear independence criteria support objective judgement and effective challenge”, MAS proposes to refine the criteria for determining whether directors are independent from management, business relationships and substantial shareholders. Currently, directors are assessed for independence based on their relationships with the FI, its subsidiaries and substantial shareholders, as well as whether they have served on the board continuously for nine years or more. The proposed criteria widens the test to cover relationships with the FI’s parent and sister companies, as well as certain business dealings involving directors’ immediate family members. Directors who have served nine years or more in total, rather than continuously, would also be deemed non-independent. MAS is also proposing that the boards of domestic systemically important banks would need at least seven directors, while full banks, domestic systemically important insurers and their parent companies would need at least five. A majority of directors would also have to be fully independent at major banks and insurers. The regulator said these refinements are intended to ensure that boards continue to have the breadth of perspectives and expertise and independent oversight needed as institutions grow in scale and complexity. Domestic systemically important banks are DBS Bank, OCBC, UOB, Citibank, Maybank, Standard Chartered Bank and HSBC. Domestic systemically important insurers consist of AIA, Income Insurance, Prudential and Great Eastern. MAS also proposes to require prior approval for additional key appointments, such as chairperson of nominating committee of locally incorporated banks and insurers, and chief information officer of domestic systematically important banks. This reflects the increasing importance of succession planning, technology and information risk management at the board and senior management levels. Another proposed change would remove the need for prior approval of certain board and senior management appointments for FIs with less retail reach or lower systemic importance, to keep regulatory requirements risk-proportionate. Overall, the proposed changes strengthen safeguards in specific areas where risks and practices have evolved, while streamlining requirements for FIs with less impact on customers and the financial system, MAS said. FIs th at are more systemically important or have greater retail reach can have a larger impact on customers and the financial system, and are therefore subject to more stringent corporate governance requirements. Interested parties have until Dec 9 to share their feedback here .

events.title: ‘Groundhog Day’: Iran is unlikely to let the war end until after the midterms—and may even escalate soon
events.summary: The seemingly endless morass of the Iran war with its rinse-and-repeat cycle of peace talks, collapsing negotiations, and modest escalations of violence is likely to continue at least through the congressional midterms in November and potentially beyond, geopolitical and energy analysts said. Why? Iranian officials—divided between public-facing politicians and the increasingly powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)—want to maximize their leverage and political harm to President Donald Trump in the election cycle. With the U.S. and Iran far apart in peace talks and more oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz under U.S. escort of late, Iran is increasingly losing, leaving them with the option of maintaining the status quo or intensifying their attacks. “It feels like ‘Groundhog Day,’” said Matt Reed, president of geopolitical and energy consultancy Foreign Reports, citing the classic Bill Murray film about repeating the same day ad nauseum. “That also might mean we’re being lulled into a false sense of security, and the situation could still deteriorate. I think this is a very dangerous moment,” Reed told Fortune . “Clearly, Iran is losing leverage, its economy is tanking, and its oil exports have collapsed. At the same time, more oil is getting out through the Strait of Hormuz than at any time since start of the war. “Combine that with the U.S. election calendar and, over the next few weeks, the Iranians might be tempted to lash out again,” he said. “If Trump is not willing to give the Iranians what they want, then their goal will be to humiliate him.” The U.S.—and much of the world—is facing seasonal record highs for gasoline prices and all-time highs for diesel costs, but any major military uptick would exacerbate prices further. With any truce or potential peace deal seemingly outside of reach for now, the Trump administration would prefer to maintain the status quo until after Nov. 3—the best choice between bad options. “I think Iran is more inclined to lash out or escalate before the election. And Trump would be more tempted to push off escalation until after,” Reed said. The benefit for the Trump administration maintaining the status quo until after the elections is that it would theoretically take away some of Iran’s leverage, said oil forecaster Dan Pickering, founder of the Pickering Energy Partners consulting and research firm. “I think the midterms are a line of demarcation. It’s just not clear to me that anything is going to happen before or after them,” Pickering said. Iran may believe Democrats winning Congress could force Trump to offer more amenable peace terms. But the United States standing pat until November could put more military options back on the table, Pickering said. “Why? This isn’t a politically popular conflict [for Trump]. Escalating the kinetic side of it post-midterms is probably more palatable,” he added.  Thierry Wizman, a top economic strategist for the Macquarie Group, said in analyst note that energy markets are preparing for exceedingly different outcomes in November. “Implied volatilities are starting to price in divergent two-way outcomes after Nov. 3, when events can shift wildly one way or the other,” Wizman stated. And more conflict means more inflation, costlier fuel prices, greater government spending, and higher bond yields. The long slog To borrow another film reference, the growing fear is the war—entering its eighth month—could evolve from “Groundhog Day” into “The NeverEnding Story.” Iran continues to demand control of the vital Strait of Hormuz—and the ability to charge tolls or fees—while the U.S. refuses to cave and is insisting on up-front nuclear concessions. “I’m not sure if there’s a peace deal—not just by the midterms—but in the next six months,” said Marshall Adkins, head of energy for Raymond James. “Getting to some kind of agreement that you can hold the IRGC to is going to be extremely difficult. They’re being patient. Are we going to be there for the next five years? Maybe, but that seems like a stretch.” Through much effort with military escorts and at a high financial cost, the U.S. is helping more oil flow out of the Middle East than almost at any time since the war began at the end of February. Export volumes are up to almost 13 million barrels of crude oil per day—while blockading Iranian shipments—but still down from 19 million barrels daily in February. Despite the increased flows, they are largely offset by China increasing its oil imports again—after dramatically cutting its imports during the summer—and the U.S. slowing to a trickle its releases from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), which is already down to 44-year lows. However, the Trump administration signed off Sept. 29 on another 40 million barrels being drained from the SPR—the culmination of which would bring the SPR down to emergency levels . “I don’t see a peace deal in the near future,” Reed said. “What I see is a lot of posturing and negotiating by force. We are not at the point yet where either side is willing to concede.” Gulf states are paying much more money for tankers and maritime insurance premiums just to move their oil volumes. A daily oil tanker charter has skyrocketed from roughly $50,000 to $1 million. And the U.S. is paying exorbitantly to fund its naval escorts. “We’re getting oil out of the strait by running these convoys, but how long are we going to do that?” Adkins asked. “Iran still has the ability to blow up a lot of stuff coming through there,” he said. “Let’s not forget, Iran could shut all this stuff down tomorrow.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Palantir CEO Alex Karp quietly purchased 37,000 acres of forests in Sweden—and locals found out when hunters lost leases to use the property
events.summary: Palantir founder and CEO Alex Karp is best known in the U.S. for his controversial $450 billion AI defense company , but in Sweden, he’s ruffled feathers for another reason: snapping up thousands of acres of land that’s disrupted local hunting. Karp has purchased 15,000 hectares (37,000 acres) of forest in Härjedalen, Sweden, through his newly registered company Cladonia Skog AB , of which he is the beneficial owner. The sale was reportedly for 235 million kronor, or $22 million. Swedish newspaper Tidningen Härjedalen first reported the deal. The outlet spoke to hunters who had received notifications in the mail alerting them they could no longer lease the land to hunt south of the quiet village of Storsjö Kapell known for its hiking and fishing. Svenska Cellulosa Aktiebolaget (SCA), a paper manufacturer that previously owned the land, confirmed it had sold the property because it was suboptimal for forestry. Banning hunting on the grounds was part of the sales agreement. “The transaction has already been completed, and terminating hunting agreements—whether for our own staff or external teams—linked to the land is a natural part of the sales process, as we can only grant hunting rights on land we own,” SCA wrote in an email to Tidningen Härjedalen .  SCA did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Karp already has ties to Sweden through Palantir, which established a partnership with Swedish defense authorities, Palantir’s Sweden Country Manager Anders Fridén confirmed earlier this year. Palantir expanded its offering software development in Europe about a decade ago, but the EU’s continued use of the company’s services has raised concerns about Europe’s plans to wean itself of U.S. technology and AI . Cladonia told Swedish media outlets it would use the land to “carry out forestry and other related activities.” Scandinavian Trust, which brokered the deal, did not respond to Fortune ’s request for comment, but has reiterated Cladonia’s intention to preserve the land. “The new owner of the forest property is committed to the beauty of the land and its preservation,” Jenny Lopes Da Silva, a board member of Cladonia and a sales manager at Scandinavian Trust, said in a statement. “The vast, natural forest landscapes offer valuable habitats for plants and animals, while also serving as a place for recreation and restoration.” Billionaire land investment Purchasing natural lands has become a popular trend for the ultrawealthy , with farmland growing into a $4.3 trillion asset class in the U.S. alone, according to Steve Bruere, president of agricultural real estate firm Peoples Company. Land is a finite resource, meaning its demand will increase over time, along with its value, making it a reliable hedge against inflation and market volatility. In the U.S., the cost of land increased 4.3% year-over-year in 2025, averaging about $4,350 per acre, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data . The rise of carbon credits , a certification that indicates action to offset greenhouse gas emissions that can be traded for emission allowances, has also incentivized owning agrarian land such as forests. But landownership has also become an elaborate hobby for some billionaires, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who is raising wagyu cattle on his 4,000 ranch in Kauai, Hawaii, and Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian, who has operated a family farm in Jupiter, Fla., for six years. “A lot of people started to appreciate the nonfinancial benefits of farmland,” Bruere previously told Fortune . “You can hike it, you can walk on it, you can fish it, you can hunt it, you can grow food on it. That trend really emerged coming out of the COVID area, where people were stuck in their homes and apartments and started looking for alternative investments.” Karp is no stranger to buying land for his own recreational purposes, which reportedly includes a 3,700 acre monastery compound in Capitol Creek Valley, Colo., which sold for $120 million , according to The Wall Street Journal . The deal also included water rights to irrigate 1,500 acres of land. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Meet Noah Shinn: The 23-year-old college dropout whose viral AI assistant is emerging as a new challenger to Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta
events.summary: At just 23 years old, Noah Shinn is already making his mark on the AI world. He founded Instinct, an AI assistant startup, just last year. Since then, its valuation has skyrocketed. The company raised $250 million at a $2.5 billion valuation in August, bringing its total raised at the time to $350 million. Just this week, the company raised an additional $1 billion in a Series C that shot its valuation up to $10 billion. Even though Instinct’s AI assistant is open only to a select few invitees, Instinct is now approaching $1 billion in annual transaction volume, Shinn said in an interview on the Invest Like the Best podcast published Monday.  Despite not being broadly available, Instinct has grown organically through word of mouth, Shinn told the podcast host and venture capitalist Patrick O’Shaughnessy. So many people want to join, he said, that existing users are now selling invitations to join Instinct on eBay .  “We spent $0 on marketing so far,” he said. What does Instinct do? Instinct is a free personal assistant powered by AI that can communicate with users via message or a phone call. The assistant launched in private beta in February, The Wall Street Journal reported, but last month opened in an invite-only beta, with each user allotted five invites. It has caught on with people who have used the tool to plan weddings and cancel hundreds of dollars worth of subscriptions, Shinn said in an X post last month. The Instinct founder said his personal assistant and others like it have the potential to simplify users’ lives, especially when it comes to travel—a category which makes up half of the billion dollars Shinn said is transacting through the platform on a yearly basis—by learning users’ preferences and storing it in its memory. “It will be able to use that memory and be able to, you know, now make it a much easier experience for you in the future to be able to book that according to exactly what you want,” he said on the podcast. Taking on Meta Instinct may have raised hundreds of millions of dollars in funding, but what may say the most about the excitement surrounding it is that the company has also caught the eye of Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang, who has poked fun at the company several times in X posts since Meta announced its own personal AI agent, Muse, earlier this month.  Wang, who became a billionaire after founding Scale AI, which Meta later put $14.3 billion into, replied to several posts comparing Muse and Instinct. In one, he said Muse would beat Instinct in an MMA match , while in another he wrote “Muse is way hotter than the other personal agents (and also way faster, but mostly hotter)” in response to another users’ post that meme’d the choice between Instinct and Muse. Wang last week replied to one more post by mocking Instinct’s name: “Muse absolutely crushes Insect,” he wrote. Shinn reportedly replied to one of Wang’s multiple posts with a smiley face. Instinct did not immediately reply to Fortune ’s request for comment. Meta did not immediately reply to Fortune ’s request for comment.  It’s unclear how many users Instinct has at the moment, but Muse, for its part, has already attracted a huge following of its own and recently replaced ChatGPT as the top free app on the U.S. App Store. Estimates from market intelligence provider Apptopia found that Muse saw 2.8 million installs worldwide in its first 12 days, TechCrunch reported . Shinn said in the interview with O’Shaughnessy that he believes Muse is a great product but that he spends “very little of my time thinking about competition and other players in the space.”  He said right now the potential for growth is huge because many people, even if they use AI, aren’t using it to its highest potential. “It’s still an exciting time,” he said.  Wang’s posts, though, may have also given Instinct a marketing boost. Combined, Wang got hundreds of thousands of views and more than 1,000 likes on his posts related to Instinct. Who is Noah Shinn? Despite the tension, Shinn and Wang have one thing  in common. Like many successful tech founders, they both dropped out of college. Shinn grew up in the San Francisco Bay Area and went to a private high school in San Jose, Business Insider reported . In high school, he played basketball and also ran cross country. He attended Northeastern University in Boston, but left in 2023 to join the startup world. But Shinn’s work on AI agents began even before he dropped out. As a student, Shinn had varied interests. He worked on type prediction and code generation in Northeastern’s Programming Language Group, researched excited-state molecular dynamics in the university’s Computational Photochemistry Group, and was also member of the avionics team in Northeastern’s student-run aerospace organization, according to his personal website . But he established himself as a serious AI researcher when he authored a paper as an undergraduate with then-Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor Ashwin Gopinath, called “Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning.” The paper explored how AI agents could learn from previous responses by having them reflect on feedback and store the data in memory to do better next time. In a blog post co-written with Gopinath, the pair wrote that their proposed method, “mirrors human problem-solving.” Shinn and his co-authors used the Reflexion approach they proposed to get a large language model to achieve 91% accuracy, compared to 80% accuracy with GPT-4, on a coding evaluation by asking it to check its responses. The paper has been cited hundreds of times, including by Google Deepmind, according to an article published by Northeastern’s Khoury College of Computer Sciences. And in 2023, Shinn and his co-authors presented their findings in 2023 at NeurIPS , a leading academic AI conference.  In 2023, Shinn also left university to join AI startup Sierra as one of the company’s first employees. Sierra, an enterprise AI intelligence platform, creates AI agents and was cofounded by OpenAI’s chairman, Bret Taylor. Instinct is now making its own AI personal assistants and competing directly with Muse, which is backed by Meta’s massive resources. Shinn meanwhile, said in a post last month the company was keeping Instinct invite only while it was “actively bringing up more compute.”  Shinn’s company may lack Meta’s enormous resources, but its rapid rise shows agents are opening up as AI’s newest battleground where opportunities abound. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Jeff Bezos is giving $25 million to protect the Pacific—but his climate fund still has about $7 billion left to spend in four years
events.summary: Back in 2020, billionaire Amazon founder Jeff Bezos pledged $10 billion to fight climate change through 2030. Nearly seven years later, the Bezos Earth Fund has granted about $2.4 billion, leaving just about four years to spend down more than $7 billion. The fund’s latest move is doling out more than $25 million in grants announced Sept. 17 to protect more than 625,000 square miles of ocean (an area larger than Alaska) across the Cook Islands, Kiribati, Papua New Guinea, Tonga, and Vanuatu. The grants are the second round of a $100 million Pacific pledge the fund made in 2023. The first round of $37.5 million went out in 2025, and the latest round brings the total awarded thus far to $63.3 million. The “Unlocking Blue Pacific Prosperity” pledge aims to sustainably manage the region’s waters and protect at least 30% of it by 2030, according to the Bezos Earth Fund. The grants are being led by Lauren Sánchez Bezos , who has served as the fund’s vice chair since its early days and has become a more visible face of the couple’s philanthropy since marrying Bezos in June 2025 . She announced the first round of Pacific grants last September, and a month later, $30 million in awards for the fund’s AI Grand Challenge , a grant program for supporting climate and environment-related innovations ranging from “decoding the songs of endangered birds to automating plant species identification,” according to the Bezos Earth Fund. This latest round of grants will help Papua New Guinea create its first large offshore marine protected area, expand protected areas in Tonga, and support the Cook Islands Marae Moana ocean park, along with habitat protection planning in Kiribati and Vanuatu. Essentially, marine protected areas limit what can happen in a stretch of ocean, and the strictest, “fully protected” areas ban fishing, mining, and other extractive activities outright, according to The MPA Guide , a framework developed with the International Union for Conservation of Nature. A grant to conservation group Rare will also help Pacific governments draft some of the first protection proposals for the high seas under the UN’s High Seas Treaty, which took effect in January and establishes a legal framework to protect marine biodiversity in international waters.  “Out there, the ocean isn’t just a beautiful view,” Sánchez Bezos said in a statement . “It’s the road, the pantry, the backyard.” It’s particularly important and timely work, given that the World Meteorological Organization said in a July report the vast ocean expanse in the South-West Pacific is becoming hotter and more acidic, harming local economies and marine ecosystems. Indeed, 2025 was the region’s second-warmest year on record, with marine heatwaves disrupting ecosystems and fisheries, according to the report. “Across Asia and the Pacific, heat is intensifying multi-hazard risks, intersecting with food systems, public health, infrastructure and oceans, and placing new pressures on health and livelihoods,” Armida Salsiah Alisjahbana, executive secretary of the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, said in a statement. The Bezos Earth Fund said it’s already seeing results from its push in the Pacific. With its latest round, 17 of the region’s 22 countries are now working to protect and sustainably manage their waters. Among the first-round recipients, French Polynesia created the world’s largest network of fully protected marine areas earlier this year. That covers nearly 625,000 square miles of ocean, and Niue has already protected 40% of its national waters.  The spending clock The Pacific grants are part of a busy stretch for the Bezos Earth Fund. Since April, it has announced $34 million to develop more sustainable fabrics , $26 million for wildfire detection and prevention, $100 million to turn vacant urban land into parks in eight U.S. cities, and $100 million toward a joint effort with Leonardo DiCaprio’s Re:wild to save the world’s most threatened species.  Still, the Bezos Earth Fund will need to stay busy through 2030 to reach its $10 billion commitment. To give away the remaining $7.6 billion by the end of 2030, it would need to average about $1.8 billion a year. The fund recently said it’s still committed to meeting its deadline. Officials told Bloomberg in May they remain committed to giving away the full $10 billion by 2030, and grantmaking had rebounded to at least $400 million this year after falling to $183 million in 2025.  “We take the time before getting into an area to understand it and make sure we’re having the greatest impact that we possibly can,” Kelly Levin , chief of science, data, and systems change at Bezos Earth Fund, told Bloomberg. And to be sure, this is all still just a drop in the bucket for Bezos. He’s worth about $272 billion, making him the world’s fourth-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index . Forbes estimates the couple’s lifetime giving at about $4.7 billion. Bezos has previously acknowledged that giving money away well is hard. “It’s not easy. Building Amazon was not easy,” he told CNN in 2022. “I’m finding … that charity, philanthropy, is very similar.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Designing Physical AI Systems Under Real-World Constraints
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Where latency, power, reliability, and data movement shape system behavior. Physical AI extends artificial intelligence into systems that sense, interpret, and act in the physical world. Unlike centralized AI infrastructure, these systems operate within bounded latency, power, thermal, reliability, and environmental constraints. They must respond to changing inputs in real time, often under conditions where delayed or inconsistent behavior can affect equipment, processes, or human safety. While Physical AI often operates at the edge, it extends beyond edge AI by combining AI inference with closed-loop interaction in the physical world, where sensing, decision-making, and actuation operate together under strict timing and operational constraints. At the center of Physical AI is a continuous sensing, inference, and response cycle. Sensor data is captured, processed, interpreted, and translated into action. Maintaining that cycle requires predictable behavior across memory, compute, communication, and I/O resources. Delays in data arrival, variability in memory access, inefficient communication, or synchronization overhead can directly affect how the system responds. Physical AI systems must move, process, and act on data within strict timing and operational constraints. Memory, communication, synchronization, and I/O are all part of the control path. Edge AI plays a central role in this architecture because many Physical AI systems cannot rely on centralized infrastructure for immediate decisions. Sensor data may be too large, too frequent, too latency-sensitive, or too safety-critical to send to a remote system before action is taken. Local execution becomes necessary, but edge environments introduce additional constraints, including limited power budgets, thermal variation, vibration, motion, shock, humidity, and other physical operating conditions. These infrastructure constraints are implemented through silicon-level decisions. Memory interfaces, interconnect, I/O subsystems, and die-to-die links carry, exchange, and synchronize data across the system. Physical AI systems also rarely operate in isolation. Devices often participate in larger architectures spanning edge, industrial, vehicle, and cloud environments, where information must be exchanged and coordinated across multiple system boundaries. The same data movement, synchronization, and infrastructure challenges extend beyond a single device and shape behavior across the broader system. events.title: Data Center Energy Trends Force A Rethink Of Chip Power Delivery
events.summary: By Kaladhar Radhakrishnan, Vishal Javvaji, and Nicolas Butzen The modern data center is facing a sharp uptick in power consumption driven by the rapid growth of AI, high-performance computing (HPC), and cloud-scale services. The training of large models, real-time inference, and data-intensive applications are driving unprecedented compute density and current demands. According to Gartner, “worldwide data center power demand is expected to rise 27% in 2026 and reach 132 gigawatts (GW), up from 104GW in 2025. It is estimated to attain 290GW by 2030, which reflects the unprecedented scale and pace of GenAI boosting demand.” AI-optimized servers continue to fuel the increase in data center power consumption. Gartner estimates “AI-optimized server adoption will account for 31% of data center power consumption in 2026, and that by 2027 their power consumption will surpass that of conventional servers.”¹ In our latest technical white paper , we take a deep dive into how power delivery is becoming one of the dominant forces shaping how systems are architected, deployed, and scaled. Traditional power delivery constraints Power efficiency is often viewed as a system-on-chip (SoC) design challenge, but in modern AI and cloud data centers, the real constraints extend well beyond the silicon itself. Nearly all projected growth in electricity demand comes from AI infrastructure and the additional cooling and support systems required to operate it. Rack-level power limits, facility power budgets, and cooling capacity increasingly dictate how much compute can be deployed, making every watt a critical resource shared across processors, memory, networking, and storage. At the same time, conventional frontside power delivery imposes a growing tax on silicon efficiency. By routing power and signals through the same metal layers, traditional architectures force competition for valuable routing resources. These challenges are further amplified by rising current demands and shrinking voltage margins. Even small increases in resistance and inductance can degrade power integrity and lead to timing failures. Designers compensate through wider power rails, additional decoupling, and larger guard bands, adding cost and complexity while delivering diminishing returns. Decoupling power and signal routing Intel Foundry is addressing these challenges with backside power delivery architectures that move power routing off the signal layers, improving routing efficiency, reducing IR drop, and enhancing performance-per-watt at advanced process nodes. Introduced with Intel 18A, RibbonFET Gate-all-around (GAA) transistor architecture with PowerVia technology makes power delivery an enabling foundation for performance. At the top end of the device portfolio, RibbonFET with Power Boost is a performance optimized dual contact device option engineered to increase available drive current through mobility enhancements and ultra-low resistance contacts, translating directly into higher achievable frequency at matched capacitance on Intel 18A-P. PowerDirect, the second generation of Intel Foundry’s backside power delivery technology planned for Intel 14A, will build on the benefits of PowerVia by introducing additional area efficiencies and a more optimized power delivery architecture, further improving overall power, performance, and area (PPA). A new power delivery architecture In a backside power delivery architecture, power is delivered physically closer to the transistors that consume it. Shorter vertical power paths reduce resistance and inductance, directly lowering IR drop and improving voltage stability. PowerVia anchors this architecture by supplying power through dedicated backside layers, while Intel Foundry’s capacitor technologies — Omni MIM (a high-density on die metal-insulator-metal capacitor) and substrate embedded MIM with through-silicon vias (eMIM-T) — provide dense, efficient near-load decoupling to support stable operation. Together, these elements allow silicon to operate closer to its true performance envelope without excessive guard banding. Fig. 1: Backside power delivery using PowerVia (Omni MIM spotlight on left). This proximity becomes especially critical for modern bursty workloads such as AI inference and HPC acceleration, where current demand shifts rapidly over short time scales. Shorter power paths enable faster transient response, reducing droop during workload spikes and improving overall energy efficiency. Technologies such as embedded deep trench capacitors (eDTC) further strengthen localized charge delivery, while advanced packaging solutions like Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge-T (EMIB-T) extend these benefits across multi‑die systems with high‑bandwidth, low‑loss interconnects. The result is a power delivery architecture designed to handle dynamic, power‑dense computing workloads driving today’s data centers. By moving power closer to the transistors and pairing it with dense, localized decoupling and system‑scale extensions, backside power delivery breaks the escalating trade‑offs between performance, efficiency, and reliability that constrain traditional designs. The result is not just cleaner power, but greater architectural freedom: tighter margins without fragility, higher utilization without excessive guard bands, and scalability without disproportionate complexity. Read our technical white paper to dive deeper into how Intel Foundry’s power delivery solutions can help scale your designs. AI failures rarely stem from one single mistake; small perception errors can silently propagate through downstream functions and affect safety critical behavior.
