events.title: Lithium plunges 25% in China on fears over battery demand growth
events.summary: The imposition of a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries and macro headwinds in the wider economy are further clouding prospects for demand. Chinese lithium futures fell 25% in September due to fears of weakening demand for electric vehicle batteries and energy storage systems. Government actions like halting new battery projects and imposing consumption taxes are dampening demand, compounded by global trade barriers and economic challenges. Despite the price drop, some analysts expect a supply deficit in coming years, suggesting the decline is sentiment-driven and may reverse soon. GUANGZHOU – Chinese lithium futures have shed a quarter of their value in September, pummelled by concerns over flagging demand. Often prone to volatile trading, the Guangzhou exchange’s contract for lithium carbonate, a refined form of the metal used in electric vehicle batteries and larger energy-storage systems (ESS), has slumped below 120,000 yuan (S$22,900) a tonne from over 160,000 yuan at the start of September. The plunge in price caps an otherwise dynamic year in 2026 for the industry in China – the world’s largest. Constraints on mine supply, strong export growth and the emergence of utility-scale batteries as a major demand driver have revived the market after it bottomed in 2025. In 2025, the Guangzhou contract was around 74,000 yuan a tonne. But optimism is starting to crumble. “There is a mounting sense of doubt that the consumption momentum can hold up to the end of 2026 sufficiently to absorb the strong cell production we have seen recently,” said Adam Megginson, principal lithium price analyst at consultancy Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. “The story here is not about immediate demand, but worries regarding demand resilience in the midterm.” Like many Chinese industries, even the successful ones, battery-makers have built too much capacity relative to demand. To address that, the government suspended in September the construction of new projects. Global trade barriers, especially in the European Union, and tighter US monetary policy pose yet more risks to the outlook. Into that mix, a private survey of Chinese inventory earlier in September confounded many in the industry by pointing to much bigger stockpiles than expected, sparking a heated debate and focusing attention on the true state of demand. The plunge in shares at Contemporary Amperex Technology, the world’s biggest EV battery-maker, has also attracted negative headlines. Still, there are those outside China who think the frayed nerves and steep price drop have been overdone. “It seems to me that the decline is based on sentiment among certain investors rather than on the market itself,” said Ignacio Mehech, chief executive officer of Chilean miner CleanTech Lithium. “There’s no market fundamental behind it, and it should reverse in the short term because analysts continue to see a deficit in the coming years,” he said in an interview in Santiago. The Chinese EV market is sluggish and there’s a growing disparity between ESS battery cell production and actual installations, said Jordan Roberts, senior analyst at consultancy Project Blue. Expectations of improved lithium supply into 2027 have also had an impact, he said. “That said, the underlying supply-demand balance still points to monthly deficits for the rest of the year, which should mean continued inventory drawdown, albeit at a slower pace, offering some support to prices,” Roberts added. The price of coal for Chinese power plants rose for an 11th straight week as officials rush to boost domestic mining and major supplier Indonesia struggles with output. Brazilian beef shipments to China face an additional 55% tariff after reaching Beijing’s annual import quota, a development that could disrupt trade between the two agricultural heavyweights and redirect global supply flows. China’s factory activity expanded for the first time since June, with a slew of indicators showing the economy ended the third quarter on a bright note as policymakers move to deploy new measures to support growth. China’s latest economic stimulus package appears designed to keep economic growth on target rather than deliver a broad revival, leaving the country’s underlying demand weakness largely unaddressed. As Qu Shaolong pulls his electric truck into one of the many charging stations that dot the Chinese coal hub of Yulin, the latest phase in the country’s energy transition is playing out in real time. events.title: Apple expected to sell 6 million units of iPhone Duo on 'bold' $1,999 price point
events.summary: Apple is expected to sell about six million units of its new foldable iPhone Duo this year, thanks to strong demand potential on its “bold” pricing, according to Counterpoint Research. The foldable device has been priced at $1,999, about $100 above the Galaxy Z Fold8. “Apple’s pricing was one of the most impressive parts of the launch,” said Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research. “Keeping the iPhone Duo just under the $2,000 mark … looks like a pretty bold move, especially for a first-generation foldable. At this price, we think demand potential could be quite strong, particularly among existing iPhone Pro series users and early adopters who have been waiting for an Apple foldable.” The six million sale mark is the estimate at the upper end and depends on how quickly production is stepped up, he said. Apple launched the iPhone Duo this month. Calling it a “thoughtful design”, the company's new chief executive, John Ternus , said: “The other products out there just look like two phones glued together side by side.” Orders for Apple's first foldable phone will begin on October 16 in the UAE, starting at Dh8,499 ($2,300) for the base model and potentially costing as much as Dh13,600 for a model with more storage. “The key challenges remain pretty much the same – durability, crease visibility, hinge reliability, thickness, weight and battery life,” said Mr Pathak. “Apple will not solve all of these overnight, but its scale and strict quality requirements should push suppliers to invest more in engineering, capacity and yield improvement. Over time, that should help improve both performance and cost across the industry.” Boost for foldables Apple's new device is expected to provided a big boost to the foldables segment, amid a wider decline in the smartphones market this year. Worldwide smartphone shipments are expected to fall 16.7 per cent this year to slightly more than one billion in what would be the steepest annual contraction the industry has recorded, according to IDC’s Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker released last month. However, the foldables category is expected to grow 12.6 per cent in 2026 to 22.9 million units, then accelerate to 18 per cent growth next year, reaching about 27 million units, IDC said. “The rapid growth is thanks to Apple’s entry into the category in the second half of this year. Apple is not only adding a new model or increasing competition in the foldables category; it is converting a segment that was about to decline into the fastest-growing part of the industry,” the report said. For the global foldable smartphone market, 2026 is expected to represent a “structural inflection point”, moving beyond a cyclical recovery towards a more sustainable expansion phase, Counterpoint said in a report earlier this year. “ The bigger message is that foldables are moving beyond being just a technology showcase and becoming a more established premium smartphone category,” Mr Pathak said. “In the end, adoption will still depend much more on better usability, thinner and lighter designs, improved durability, stronger software and whether consumers feel the extra price is worth.”

events.title: Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years
events.summary: Published 30 September 2026, 00:03 BST Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276, figures shared with the BBC reveal. The 16% predicted increase would hit millions of households at the coldest time of year, and would mark the biggest rise in bills for four years. The forecast from consultancy Cornwall Insight comes a day before prices go up under regulator Ofgem's October price cap and puts increased pressure on the government to support those who will struggle to pay. Meanwhile, the boss of supplier EDF Simone Rossi has warned the UK is "walking into a second energy crisis" and called for an extension to the VAT cut on electricity which kicks in on Thursday. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he would not call Rossi's crisis warning an overstatement, adding that the cost of home energy, as well as petrol and diesel, was "very difficult indeed". Speaking from the Labour conference in Liverpool, he added: "We're looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off." About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity. Those homes will see a 4% increase in prices on Thursday, the equivalent of about £60 per year – or £5 per month – taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year. That rise would have been higher without the government's VAT cut, which knocks the equivalent of about £45 a year off a typical bill. But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggests the typical annual bill would rise to £1,999. The forecast 16% rise will come at the worst time of year, according to Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight. "These prices are going to hit households hard. January is already a difficult month for many, with cold weather and bank balances still recovering from Christmas," he said. The predicted rise is the result of disruption of gas supplies owing to the conflict in the Middle East, and the resulting low gas storage levels in Europe. Rebuilding those stocks could mean high bills "well beyond the winter", the forecaster said. Cornwall Insight has a strong track record on forecasts and is widely respected across the industry and politics. Similar forecasts have been made by energy suppliers. What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 1 day ago Four ways to keep your energy bills down Published 1 day ago This remains only a prediction at this stage. Ofgem will not announce the actual January price change until late November. While an easing of tensions in the Middle East could lessen the pain for billpayers, the price setting period for the January cap is already halfway through. With little sign of a truce or lower international energy costs, a big increase in prices for those not on a fixed tariff looks highly likely. Lowrey said a January rise was "all but certain". Aaron Richards says it feels like all his costs are going up That will be tough for people like Aaron Richards from Maidenhead. "I try to eat less takeaways, work more overtime, and try to budget a bit better, but at the same time, we shouldn't have to," he said. Aaron drives a diesel car, and so is paying record high prices to travel to and from work. "I just feel like everything's going up. How far is it going to go? Someone's got to step in," he said. "I know people who can't afford to heat their house and they're struggling at the moment. Housing and eating are two of life's essentials that everyone should have. It shouldn't be a challenge to have any of those things." Years of relatively high domestic energy bills have left some people facing big sums in unpaid bills. Recent data from Ofgem showed that customers collectively owe more than £5bn in unpaid bills and charges to suppliers. The regulator has a proposed debt relief scheme on the table, and campaigners keep telling them to get on with it, urging the government to provide funding for it to be implemented. "This is unsustainable, not just for households but also for the market as a whole," said Adam Scorer, chief executive of fuel poverty charity National Energy Action. "The Budget must deliver additional targeted support for households most at risk this winter, alongside action to tackle energy debt and improve the least energy-efficient homes." events.title: Drop in donations puts community pantry at risk
events.summary: St Paul's Pantry in Norton Lees has had to expand into the church building to accommodate all the people that use the food bank Volunteers at a community pantry say they fear they may have to close unless they can bring in additional donations of money and food. Tina Sampson-Smith from St Paul's community pantry, in Norton Lees, Sheffield, said a drop off in donations and a rise in demand had left them in a precarious situation. Asked how the coming weeks and months looked she replied: "They look pretty grim at the moment." According to the Trussell Trust more than 2.2m food parcels were given out in England in 2025, a 56% rise on 2019. Sampson-Smith said: "I looked at our freezers yesterday and the majority of them are off because we do not have the food stock in them. "It's always tough from September to November, but this year is tougher than ever." She said, in recent weeks, one day the pantry had 204 people turn up in need of support. "Food poverty is really, really high at the moment and it's a never-ending battle to get food because our supermarkets haven't got the stock to give us," she said. Co-founder Jay Judge said: "It's a day to day battle "[There's] more and more people in food poverty, those that you see and those that you don't see. "For every person that turns up at the pantry there's a family behind that. "We might be seeing over 200 people coming through the door but it's feeding a lot more people than that." Sampson-Smith added: "We provided school lunches during the school holidays, but at this point in time we've nothing in our freezers to do that for half term." The community pantry welcomed 204 people one Wednesday morning Jenny Farrall‑Bird, area manager for charity the Trussel Trust, said this time of year was especially demanding for food banks. She said some families on the lowest incomes were going to have to make decisions such as whether to "prioritise feeding their children over themselves", skipping meals and choosing not to heat their homes. "Food banks are really a lifeline for people in financial crisis," she said. The rising cost of food has also led to a significant drop in donations over recent years, she added. "Food banks are having to do more fundraising and to get income to buy food stock so they can pass that on to people." Sampson-Smith said, as well as providing food parcels and meals, the community pantry also provide a space for people to speak with a cost of living worker and family hub workers. Appealing for support she said: "We really want to continue. We don't want to stop what we're doing." events.title: JPMorgan, Goldman See Mideast Oil Flows Near Pre-War Levels
events.summary: Crude oil flows from the Middle East are returning toward pre-war levels despite continued risks to shipping, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. Shipments of crude oil have rebounded to 98% of pre-war levels, while flows of products such as diesel and gasoline were at 58%, according to JPMorgan. Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs said oil exports from the Persian Gulf had recovered to 23.3 million barrels a day over the last week, in line with the 2025 average. Bloomberg's Stuart Livingstone-Wallace breaks down the situation. (Source: Bloomberg)

events.title: Sydney Airport near-collision one of worst in 20 years, investigators say
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sydney Airport runway conflict in July one of Australia's most severe, safety investigator says The ATSB has released preliminary reports into four of the six incidents at Sydney Airport between July and August. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The Australian Transport Safety Bureau on Wednesday released preliminary reports related to four out of six incidents at Sydney Airport. The ATSB identified a July 27 incident as one of the most severe to occur since safety records began in 2003. The final findings into the occurrences between July and late-August will be handed down at a later date. A near-collision at Sydney Airport in July has been deemed one of the most severe runway conflicts since record-keeping began more than 20 years ago, air safety investigators say. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) on Wednesday released four preliminary reports related to six incidents that occurred at Kingsford Smith Airport between July and August . The reports do not make findings or recommendations, but outline the sequence of events and key operational context at the time of the incidents. Angus Mitchell deemed the July 27 incident at Sydney Airport a Category A event. ( ABC News ) ATSB Commissioner Angus Mitchell said the first of the incidents, involving two Qantas aircraft in July, had been deemed a "Category A runway incursion". He said the event was the most severe to occur in Sydney and was only the third such incident within Australia since ATSB records began in 2003. An illustration of QLK424D and QF124 on the July 27 incident. ( Source: ATSB ) On July 27, a "breakdown of coordination" led an air traffic controller to clear a Boeing 737 (QF124) carrying 157 people to cross a runway as a QantasLink Bombardier (QLK424D) with 55 people onboard was landing. The interim report said the air controller who issued the clearance had a "high predicted fatigue risk level" when a brief handover was given to another controller while they went on break. "[The 737] had stopped before reaching the intersection of runway 34L and runway 25 but was within the runway surface area past the runway stop bars, resulting in a runway incursion," the report said. "[The Bombardier] came to a stop prior to the runway 34L and 25 runway intersection. When both aircraft came to a stop, they were approximately 120 m apart." The report also said that, the time of the occurrence, Sydney's air traffic control tower was operating with high predicted fatigue levels for four out of seven controllers. "Whilst an elevated fatigue risk does not necessarily mean a controller was fatigued, or that fatigue affected performance, we are, however, examining the effectiveness of the measures that were in place to manage this pre-identified risk," Mr Mitchell said. Four traffic controllers had a "high predicted fatigue risk level" at the time of the July incident. ( ABC News ) Mr Mitchell said roster modelling by Airservices Australia had predicted an "elevated fatigue risk" for staff on many of the days in which conflicts occurred between July 27 and August 25. Mr Mitchell said while staff resourcing was not determined as the direct cause of the occurrences, the ATSB would investigate whether the practice of combining operational roles and an over-reliance on overtime to fill shifts were underlying factors. On Wednesday, the ATSB also released a report comparing levels of similar occurrences across Australian airports between 2016 and 2026 to ascertain whether the incidents at Sydney Airport were localised or reflected a broader national trend. Mr Mitchell said between July and August this year there had been 11 ground incidents reported at Sydney Airport, including the six currently under investigation. Sydney also reported double the annual average of "information and procedural errors" compared to other major airports nationally, he said. An interim report has also been released into a near-miss at Sydney Airport on August 9. ( Supplied ) Mr Mitchell said "higher consequence incidents", such as runway incursions, taxiway collisions and losses of separation, had also increased post-COVID. "Nationally, occurrence rates have remained steady over the past decade, at Sydney, however, ground conflictions attributed to ATC actions have increased since the COVID-19 recovery," he said. Mr Mitchell said challenges from COVID were still impacting operations, not only in Australia but globally. "It's not just these incidents, we have seen those impacts at times with delays in flights [and] at times some of the stressors within the system and the flow on effects.

events.title: Russia lost one of its irreplaceable Tu-95 nuclear-capable bombers in a deadly training crash
events.summary: The Tu-95 turboprop aircraft forms the backbone of Russia's long-range nuclear bomber fleet. ALEXANDER NEMENOV/AFP via Getty Images Russia said on Tuesday that a Tu-95 bomber crashed in one of its eastern regions. At least six crew members died during the crash, which occurred during training, per state media. The crash is a blow to Russia's nuclear bomber fleet, with Tu-95s now out of production. One of Russia's Tu-95 strategic bombers crashed during a training flight in the Amur region, killing six crew members, the country's defense ministry said on Tuesday. The plane was not carrying any ammunition, and a seventh crew member survived the initial crash and was hospitalized, the defense ministry added, per state media. "A Tu-95 military aircraft made an emergency landing while conducting a training flight near Krasnoyarovo. The crew did everything possible to divert the aircraft away from residential buildings," the ministry said in a statement. According to state media, the bomber went down shortly after taking off from the Ukrainka air base. The Amur region is in eastern Russia, bordering China's Heilongjiang province. Russian officials have not said what caused the crash. The Russian defense ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent by Business Insider. Russia is believed to possess 47 Tu-95MS bombers , though Ukrainian intelligence said in August that combat losses, maintenance issues, and a shortage of parts have reduced its operational fleet to 37 or 38 planes. The crash comes more than a year after Ukraine conducted a surprise drone attack, Operation Spiderweb , on a Russian air base in June 2025 that damaged an estimated seven to eight Tu-95 aircraft. The turboprop aircraft, capable of flying up to 9,300 miles without extra fueling, forms the backbone of Russia's air-based nuclear attack capability and is often compared to the American B-52 Stratofortress . The B-52 Stratofortress forms the backbone of the US' nuclear bomber fleet. Leon Neal/Getty Images Losing one of these bombers is a significant blow to Russia's long-range nuclear attack fleet. The Kremlin can no longer make any more of these aircraft, after dismantling production facilities in the 1990s as the Soviet Union collapsed. The Tu-95MS can carry up to 16 nuclear or conventional missiles at a time, and Russia has more recently used the bomber to launch Kh-101 and Kh-555 precision cruise missiles at Ukraine from far behind the front lines. The fleet is supplemented by about 18 Tu-160 bombers , which are heavier, more modern aircraft with jet engines capable of supersonic speeds. Moscow is actively building these newer aircraft, but production has been slow as Russia faces international sanctions on high-end parts, with one or two planes delivered a year, if any. The Tu-160 is Russia's modern nuclear bomber. AFP via Getty Images About two-thirds of these Tu-160s are also believed to be grounded for maintenance and upgrades, per Ukrainian open-source analysts who monitor satellite imagery and registries of Russia's airfields and aircraft workshops. Ukraine said last year that Operation Spiderweb had also struck four Tu-160s, though satellite imagery has only shown that one or two of them sustained repairable damage. Russia also fields the Tu-22M3 supersonic nuclear bomber, which can only fly roughly half as far as a Tu-95. It started the war with about 41 Tu-22M3 aircraft on its service registry, but attrition from Ukrainian attacks and crashes has whittled its estimated operational fleet down to as few as nine flightworthy planes. events.title: OpenAI unveils AI assistant 'dots' while safety worries delay new model
events.summary: Sam Altman has spoken repeatedly in recent weeks about the risks posed by AI agents. OpenAI on Tuesday unveiled "dots", a new artificial intelligence (AI) assistant it says can proactively carry out tasks on a user's behalf. At its annual developer day in San Francisco, chief executive Sam Altman referred to "dots" as "remarkably capable, always-on agents that can handle really anything you can think of." At the same time, OpenAI president Greg Brockman and other tech leaders held a meeting with President Donald Trump as the firm faces intense scrutiny after internal tests of its AI agents revealed unexpected and occasionally harmful actions. Dots, however, were pitched as brightly coloured cute cartoons meant to function as digital assistants for people with busy lives. The dots, Altman said, "can handle really anything you can think of." A glossy video was shown during the event, with people speaking to and naming animated versions of their "dots," then giving them various tasks, like building a website and booking afterschool activities for their children. Speaking about "my dot," Altman almost entirely eschewed referring to the tool as an agent, which has been in common use for years. AI agents are essentially AI chatbots that are programmed to operate somewhat autonomously. "You just give your dot a responsibility... and your dots will just get to work and keep working," Altman added. At the event, Altman reiterated his decision for OpenAI to not make a highly anticipated stock market debut until it can "make confident safety decisions". The company has been preparing for a blockbuster listing, potentially valuing the firm at up to $1.4tn (£1.06tn). Altman told reporters that "it is going to take us some time to figure out how to make sure that alignment, monitoring, safety, security stay well ahead of capabilities." OpenAI's event on Tuesday took place as President Donald Trump held a White House lunch with tech leaders and House Speaker Mike Johnson. Trump repeated his belief that AI companies should regulate themselves. He also said they had discussed creating a ten-person committee to oversee the sector, adding there would be "tremendous self-policing" Some researchers and company heads have called for a slowdown in AI development as more instances of breaches by AI firms' models become public. "We need to navigate the centrist path," Altman told the BBC during a question and answer session with reporters on Tuesday. "I am hopeful that the industry will figure out a more sensible, more pragmatic stance than has been exhibited by some of the members of our industry," he added, declining to specify particular company names or leaders. The day prior to OpenAI's event, the company said it was delaying the launch of its latest model due to certain safety issues that showed up during internal testing. Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit Published 4 hours ago OpenAI scraps rollout of new model over safety concerns Published 22 hours ago Since July, the company has been dealing with a series of issues with its AI agents acting improperly. It has faced unprompted hacking into the AI platform Hugging Face, posting to third-party websites images that AI agents took from ChatGPT user chats, and accessing non-public information maintained by the Australian government . OpenAI, as well as rival AI firm Anthropic, previously delayed public release of certain AI models due to potential risks, mostly pertaining to cybersecurity or hacking concerns. On Tuesday, Altman raised the possibility of "a legitimate loss of control" to an AI system, adding "and you can imagine where we have too much concentration of power in a small number of companies or one company or person or country or whatever". Both OpenAI and Anthropic are expect to be listed on the public stock market in the coming months. Anthropic likely will do so this year, while OpenAI is poised for 2027. Altman said he was eager for his company to sell shares in public markets. "I think it's bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public," Altman told reporters. "I want people to be able to part in the upside of AI." Both companies have lately been clear that they believe AI poses a genuine risk on a large scale, be it to public infrastructure or public safety. Speaking last week to the UN, Altman pleaded for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained. Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, told the UN that if the speeding development of AI was not properly managed and overseen, future versions of the technology "could be a risk to humanity as a whole." events.title: Risks being taken with heating oil orders, firm says
events.summary: Supplier Dave Marsh said customers might be leaving it too late to refill their tanks Heating oil customers who are worried about the cost are taking risks by delaying orders in the hope of a price fall, a firm has warned. Marsh Fuels, which supplies heating oil in Berkshire and Hampshire, said its sales were lower than expected as colder weather approaches. However, the firm said customers could run out of oil or expose themselves to even higher bills by waiting. UK heating oil prices have risen by about 75% since the start of the Iran conflict on 28 February, according to the BoilerJuice website , external . Dave Marsh from the Newbury-based firm said: "We're coming into autumn and we would expect to be busier than we are. "And so we've made the assumption that customers are hanging on, trying to eke out that little bit of oil they've still got left in the bottom of their tank, hoping for the price to dip. "The problem is that can be quite risky. If we get a cold snap and the customers are lower than they think they are, they may suddenly be urgent." Andrew Illingworth said heating oil orders had fallen in his village Andrew Illingworth, who buys oil on behalf of residents in Broughton, Hampshire, said he was handling fewer orders than normal for the time of year. "A lot of them are holding off at the moment," he said. "They're hoping that it's going to go back down again, but who knows at the moment." Chris Wheeler, from Bucklebury, Berkshire, said the price volatility, including surges and dips, was "frustrating". "You never know what's going to happen," he said. "Except at the moment all you can expect is that the price is going to go up. "So we're trying to manage our purchases so that we can buy it when it's at its cheapest." Chris Wheeler said he planned to buy oil when the price dropped Ellen Fraser, energy expert at the Baringa consultancy, said she would buy oil now. She told the Money Box programme on BBC Radio 4: "We're expecting those prices to stay high until at least April and May, which is obviously far too late to fill the tank." The Fuel Distribution Association (UKIFDA) previously said customers should prepare for periods of increased demand, severe weather or unexpected delivery delays. Chief executive Ken Mackness said: "The events we saw earlier this year demonstrated how quickly international developments can affect wholesale energy markets." In March, the government announced a £50m emergency fund , external to help struggling families with heating oil costs. events.title: Hegseth to cut number of US general and admiral positions by 20%
events.summary: Pentagon official says the plan will be announced in the defence secretary’s ‘State of the Force’ address in Virginia. United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will cut the number of positions reserved for generals and admirals by 20 percent, a Pentagon official has told Al Jazeera, in a change that will affect leadership across the Army, Navy and Air Force. Hegseth is expected to announce the decision on Wednesday during a visit to the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, where he will deliver his “State of the Force” address in front of junior officers and enlisted officials, the official said. list 1 of 3 Why has the Trump administration ordered staff to take polygraph tests? list 2 of 3 Republican congressman calls to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth list 3 of 3 Pentagon resumes mandatory testosterone testing for US troops over 30 Media outlets in the US have also reported on the move. The Associated Press news agency, citing Pentagon officials, reported that Hegseth will direct all the military services to double the 10 percent reduction that he ordered last year to the roughly 800 flag and general officer positions. This would make it a 20 percent total decrease and is to be completed by January 1, 2027. Fox News reported the new reductions could include any one-star general or above or officer of equivalent Navy rank. The Washing Post reported that the cuts could affect the careers of “hundreds of current and rising military leaders following scores of firings and denied promotions”. US President Donald Trump or Hegseth have fired, or pushed into retirement, more than two dozen military leaders since taking office in January 2025, including the Army’s top uniformed officer, General Randy George , in April. The administration also fired the only two women serving as four-star officers, along with several other senior female officers. Other top officials have left through retirements and resignations, including the Army secretary, Dan Driscoll , who resigned this month after repeated clashes with Hegseth. When the defence secretary first announced the effort to trim the highest levels of the military ranks, he argued it was intended to remove “redundant force structure to optimise and streamline leadership”. And in a memo released in May 2025, he added that his aim was to free the military from “unnecessary bureaucratic layers”. At this time last year, Hegseth also declared an end to “woke” culture and announced new directives for troops that included “gender-neutral” or “male-level” standards for physical fitness. Senator Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, expressed concern over Hegseth’s latest move in a statement. He said eliminating senior leadership positions must be done in consultation with Congress and warned that the planned cuts “should alarm every American”. “Congress has been clear with the Secretary that he must consult this body and explain his reasoning for senior officer removals and promotion holds. To date, we have not received satisfactory answers,” Reed said. “Our military is conducting major operations around the world, and the force is already under strain,” he added. The number of general officer positions is set by law, but positions can be left unfilled if the administration does not submit nominees to Congress.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Red Hat, Nvidia, OpenAI and friends are working on an enterprise edition they say is ‘Kubernetes for agents’ Fedora 45 beta drags the Linux console into the 21st century 13 days ago CERN moves thousands of accelerator control computers to Debian 26 days ago Insider: Red Hat is capping devs' bot budgets 28 days ago OpenClaw 2.0 pours glitter on slow-burning security dumpster fire 29 days ago The balkanization of virtualization will de-throne VMware, which doesn't mind a bit August 31, 2026 The OpenClaw project has started work on an enterprise edition in the hope that businesses lose their fear of the agentic AI project. OpenClaw was one of the first “AI harnesses” – tools that use a large language model to create a digital assistant that automates tasks. If users allow OpenClaw to access their email account, it can analyze messages and fire off AI-generated replies, even responding to meeting invitations and reserving time in a calendar app. The tool is the creation of developer Peter Steinberger, who released it to initial acclaim – and then consternation as security analysts found OpenClaw was a mess. Analyst firm Gartner labelled the project a source of “ unacceptable cybersecurity risk ” for business users, and China’s Computer Emergency Response Team warned of “extremely weak default security configurations.” That didn’t stop OpenAI hiring Steinberger and making OpenClaw the center of its plans to build personal AI agents. Speaking of OpenAI, news of work on OpenClaw Enterprise (OCE) came from a post by one of its staffers, Kevin Lin, who admitted “actual deployment of persistent agents remains limited.” “The main feedback we hear from organizations is that a stronger common security, safety, and governance standard is needed before agents can be fully adopted. As a consequence, the default stance of IT in most organizations is to ban agentic platforms like OpenClaw altogether.” “This is the problem we are trying to solve with OCE: how do we safely deploy powerful agents without nerfing their capabilities in enterprise environments?” Lin said work on version 1.0 of OCE is under way and that it “introduces an enterprise-grade control plane for agents and builds upon the foundation set by OpenClaw with support for multi-tenancy, hard security boundaries, and standardized agentic primitives.” “OCE adds governance and auditability across the agent lifecycle while making sure that core primitives like the harness, model, and sandbox can be swapped out with third party solutions as well as internal implementations.” Lin said work on the project “originally started at OpenAI and then was donated to the OpenClaw Foundation.” Joe Fernandes, veep and general manager of Red Hat’s AI Business Unit, likened OCE to RHEL and OpenShift, in that Red Hat intends to make an open source project suitable for serious use. “Linux helped enterprises move applications from proprietary Unix systems and specialized hardware onto an open operating system running on industry-standard infrastructure,” he wrote in a Tuesday post . “Later, containers and Kubernetes helped drive another transformation toward cloud-native applications composed of distributed microservices.” That mention of Kubernetes is likely no accident, as the OCE GitHub repo urges coders to think of the project as “Kubernetes for agents.” If OCE can achieve anywhere near the industry acceptance of Kubernetes, it will have done very well indeed. OCE emerged on the same day that OpenAI debuted its own “ dots ” personal agents, and in the same month that Meta delivered a product called “Muse” that offers OpenClaw-like automation for individuals and small businesses.

events.title: Andy Burnham wants to review the UK’s relationship with the EU. What are the options?
events.summary: The PM said Brexit has ‘done more harm than good’ and wants an assessment before the next UK-EU summit Andy Burnham has said Brexit has “done more harm than good” and pledged to launch a major review of the UK’s relationship with the EU, opening the door to a potential referendum over rejoining the union. He said he would “lay out options” around the time of the next EU-UK summit, due to be held at the end of November or soon after. While he didn’t specify options, he did not explicitly rule out rejoining. Keir Starmer’s red lines of not rejoining the single market or customs union could now also be up for discussion within Labour’s ranks in the coming weeks. “I would be stunned if Starmer’s red lines are in the next manifesto,” said Joël Reland, senior research fellow at UK in a Changing Europe , a key Brexit thinkthank. What exactly did Burnham say on the EU? “Brexit hasn’t given us control,” he said, arguing the UK had not just lost control of immigration – contrary to what Brexiters had promised – but also over the economy. “I will take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long term relationship with our European partners,” he said. “There are different options and I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in.” Going beyond Starmer’s reset ambitions is a risky move and will test Burnham’s ability to sell any closer relationship with EU to a country still bruised by Brexit. The stakes are high. In the 10 years since the Brexit referendum, the UK has drifted from its nearest trading bloc. The UK has seen exports to the EU drop, travel restrictions for British passport holders and even potential new red tape for employers who send staff to the continent on short-term contracts. A fight is under way to prevent the UK from being further locked out from trade by being included in coming Made in Europe legislation designed to protect European supply chains from cheap Chinese imports. So far it has the backing of the Netherlands, Italy and Germany but not France. Rejoining the EU would require a referendum in the UK and potentially years of de-Brexit negotiations. Plus, Brussels would need some cast iron guarantees that the UK wouldn’t just walk out again. It would mean a return to freedom of movement allowing EU citizens to live and work in the UK, and vice versa – viewed as unchecked immigration by Brexiters – but would also offer total freedom to trade without checks on standards of goods or customs forms, adding a potential 3-5% to GDP, according to the UKICE’s analysis. Switzerland is not a member of the EU but it struck a deal last year cementing its “frictionless access” to the single market, access to the EU’s electricity market, space programmes, Erasmus and the Digital Europe research programme, and participation in the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. In exchange, Switzerland agreed to free movement of people and to pay €375m (£322m) a year into the EU’s economic and cohesion funds. The EU has previously offered the UK a Swiss-style deal but it was rejected by Boris Johnson because it required regulatory alignment and free movement. Joining Norway and Liechtenstein in the EEA could add 2-3% to growth but would mean joining the single market and the customs union, two of Starmer’s red lines, and accepting immigration of EU citizens again. The single market brings with it four freedoms of movement – labour (people), capital (money), services and trade (goods). Although many have reported that the EU’s offer to Canada was the first time associate membership has come up, it is not. The EU can work expediently when the political need is there and three years ago mooted associate membership for Ukraine as a shortcut to the long accession process. This could be an option that allows the UK a closer relationship than it currently has with the EU, with less requirement to cross previously stated red lines. What is behind Burnham’s promise to redefine the UK’s relationship with Europe? Labour already sees the relationship with the EU as a point of difference with the staunchly pro-Brexit Reform UK, but has felt nervous of handing Nigel Farage free political capital by suggesting Brexit could be reversed, or at the very least heavily watered down. But sources say there is now a recognition in the Labour party that the offer to the public has got to be bigger than the current reset. How long has Burnham got to set out a fresh Brexit review? Time is short. Burnham has said he wants to have the conversation about the options over the next two months to coincide with the delayed EU-UK summit to be held in Brussels, perhaps at the end of November.

events.title: AI broke the job application. What replaces it?
events.summary: Candidates can use AI to create endless resumes and cover letters. It's forcing businesses to rethink how they hire. Skills, rather than employment history, will increasingly determine who gets hired, according to one CEO. But AI can also help with hiring, for example, by surfacing candidates from different backgrounds and reducing human bias. The resume is "broken," according to Barb Hyman, London-based founder and CEO of recruitment platform Sapia.ai. "How many people are you missing out on because you're relying on an artefact?" Hyman said, adding that AI can now tailor a resume — or CV, as it's known in the U.K. — to any role. U.K. graduate employers received an average of 140 applications per vacancy in 2025, the highest level recorded in three decades, according to data from the Institute of Student Employers . In a crowded market where candidates can use AI to create endless resumes and cover letters, finding the right person may be harder than ever. Skills, rather than employment history, will increasingly determine who gets hired, according to Hyman. A hairdresser, for example, might not look like an obvious fit for a contact center job on paper, she told CNBC, but could excel in the role because hairdressers tend to have high levels of empathy, listen to people all day and spend hours solving complex problems. Assessing skills directly can reveal strengths and weaknesses that a traditional resume hides, according to Hyman — sometimes painting a picture even the candidates themselves weren't sure of. Hyman isn't alone in seeing hiring move in this direction. Around two-thirds of U.K. organizations have adopted skills-based hiring, according to 2026 research from Michael Page , a recruitment firm headquartered in Surrey, England. Almost 60% of candidates said they were more likely to apply for roles defined by skills rather than traditional qualifications or career history. It's leading employers to think carefully about which skills they actually value. James Broadhead, the Dublin-based CTO of AI decision-making company Taktile, told CNBC that a prototype that might once have taken an engineer three weeks to build can now be one of 10 generated in a single afternoon, thanks to AI. "The hard part has become having the judgement to decide which of those are any good," Broadhead said. Taktile now looks for interpersonal skills — like how well candidates can speak to customers — as well as self-reflection and a willingness to question what they have built, he added. It's also interested in whether candidates are continually experimenting with AI. "The pace of model releases is so fast that the ceiling of what you can do changes every three months," Broadhead said. "And so the question we're asking is: what have you changed about your AI tools in the last three weeks?" Other companies are assessing potential hires by throwing them in at the deep end. At digital marketing and advertising agency PMG, graduate candidates are asked to complete practical exercises in person, work in teams and tackle client briefs. Josh Krichefski, PMG's London-based EMEA president, told CNBC this is designed to assess how candidates actually interact and approach work. "You don't really know whether someone's going to have the skills to do something until you challenge them to do it," Krichefski said. "The past doesn't tell you that." Younger candidates are often well placed for this, he said, because Gen Z has fewer preconceived notions about what a job looks like. "It's another reason for why we believe in investing in young people, particularly when we're at a time where the world's changing so bloody fast," Krichefski said. "Graduates don't arrive with fixed assumptions about how work has traditionally been done." Perhaps paradoxically, AI — despite exacerbating some of the problems with traditional hiring — can also be used to help find solutions. For example, the technology can be used to help surface candidates from different backgrounds. Sapia.ai's Hyman argues that resumes and conventional interviews have always been vulnerable to human bias, including "mirror hiring," where hiring managers consciously or unconsciously favor people with backgrounds similar to their own. "We see things through the prism of our own experience," she said. "Really what's broken is human bias, but we're all in denial about it." For Hyman, that doesn't mean taking humans out of hiring altogether. The final decision should rest with the people who will work alongside the new hire, while technology is better suited to screening candidates at scale. Assessment, she said, should always run both ways. "Hiring the wrong person is extremely painful for the hiring manager and they're best placed to know whether you're the right person for them and their team," she said. "And the job seeker deserves to get as much opportunity to stress test you, as you do of them."

events.title: Facing the future without the 'bank of mum and dad'
events.summary: Chari said she was having to use the money she had saved for the future to survive now The prime minister used the plight of young people unable to rely on the "bank of mum and dad" as a curtain-raiser for Labour's annual conference. The Your First Home scheme will offer a government-backed loan of 20% of the purchase price - with a minimum deposit of 2.5%. But how tough are things at the moment for young people who have left school and want to make their way in the world? Chari said choosing financial stability over pursuing a dream was "heartbreaking" Chari, 19, from Hertfordshire, spent some of her childhood in care but has just started at university and has ambitions to qualify as a doctor of psychology. The challenge at the moment is just getting through the next few years, she says. "I receive universal credit and that's usually what I would use to pay for my housing in Hertfordshire, but they've cut it off this month because I'm moving to university and they think SFE [the student loan] will cover it. "SFE is delayed, so I have no money this month whatsoever - I'm three days in and already I'm in debt." She added: "I'm dipping into savings I had planned to afford a future for myself just to get by now. "As a care leaver, you don't really get that chance to save money for your future or make future plans." Chari believes her dream of a doctorate may have to be put on hold while she pursues a career - and a salary - in banking. "It's heart-breaking," she said, adding: "I don't think somebody should have to choose financial stability over pursuing their dream." Elliot does not believe they will ever earn enough money to own a house Elliot, 18, is also from Hertfordshire and is living with their parents, but wants to move on. "I've been looking for places because I'm in college and I plan on going to uni, but it's just that things keep rising and the bills keep getting more and more," they said. "I don't think I've ever expected to be able to buy a house at all. It would be nice to own my own place, but will I actually earn enough to be able to?" As they turn 19 within a couple of months, Elliot believes they will have to pay for their studies. "It's about £1,500 to £2,000 just for the course and I've got to get there and back every day," they said. "In the area that I live, one of the main things is if you don't have the education, you're probably not going to get out of the place. "It's quite a low-income area. I would like to go to uni but I think 'can I afford it?'" The government said the Your First Home scheme would "help tackle the deposit barrier for first-time buyers who would be unable to afford their first home otherwise, building on the government's existing work to help more young people and families onto the housing ladder". The Conservatives warned that the policy could leave first-time buyers taking on more debt and risked "pushing up the price of new homes". But the prime minister said it would aim to help those who did not have support from the "bank of mum and dad". Burnham said: "Too many young people are struggling with the cost of housing, with many giving up hope of ever having a home to call their own. "So we will step in to help more first-time buyers on to the housing ladder." Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below. events.title: Israel’s Lapid accuses Netanyahu of ‘fear-mongering’ over attack warning
events.summary: Opposition leader dismisses Netanyahu’s warning of possible attacks during next month’s general election. Israel’s opposition leader Yair Lapid has accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of “fear-mongering” after the incumbent leader warned that the country’s enemies may attack before next month’s general election . Lapid, who heads the Yesh Atid party, dismissed the warning after meeting the prime minister on Tuesday. list 1 of 3 Satellite images show Gaza in ruins three years into Israel’s genocidal war list 2 of 3 Israeli settlers attack Jalud village in occupied West Bank pogrom list 3 of 3 Palestine weekly: Israeli politicians vie to look toughest before election Earlier in the day, Netanyahu posted an online video that showed him posing in front of a fighter jet at a military base and saying there were “indications that, ahead of the elections, our enemies will try to attack us”. He did not specify which enemy he had in mind. But in recent weeks, he has issued warnings to Iran, Hamas, Hezbollah and the Palestinian Authority, promising retaliation in the event of an attack. Lapid requested an urgent security briefing after the warning, and in an online post afterwards, he said he was certain the election would take place on time and that “there is no reason to panic the public”. “The elections will take place on time, and no one has an excuse to disrupt them,” he said. He accused Netanyahu of using military bases as “props for election campaign videos” and of failing to heed warnings before the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, which set off Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. More than 76,000 Palestinians have been killed in the war. “Netanyahu ignored every warning before October 7, and now, 28 days before the election, he’s suddenly busy fear-mongering,” Lapid said. He added: “I of course will not violate the confidentiality of the security briefing but it must be said — security threats must be handled professionally and responsibly.” The election, scheduled for October 7, is Israel’s first vote since the Hamas-led attacks, which plunged the Middle East into turmoil as Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, or is defeated by centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, was first elected prime minister in 1996. In recent weeks, he has had to deny media reports that his partners in the Middle East warned him of a potential Hamas attack, an allegation his political rivals have seized on. Polls show him in a close race to stay in power. According to a Reuters polling average, no candidate has a clear path to power. The average shows Yashar, the party of Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who has emerged as Netanyahu’s most formidable rival, leading the prime minister’s right-wing Likud party by 2 points. Based on the average, parties opposed to Netanyahu would hold 64 seats in the 120-member Knesset, 15 more than the parties that back him, but they may be unable to form a coalition. Lapid is one of several opposition figures in the race. He, Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have agreed to coordinate to remove Netanyahu’s government. Under the agreement announced last week, each leader pledged to work in their constituencies to increase turnout and attract support from various sectors of society to secure a majority and form a new government. The prime minister said in a separate post on Tuesday that he has held a security briefing with Lapid in which he raised alerts about possible attacks “on the various fronts ahead of the elections”. He stressed that he holds regular briefings with the opposition leader.

events.title: OpenAI named its new agent system Dots. It’s already causing confusion.
events.summary: OpenAI may have picked an all-too-common name for its new AI agent system. Heather Diehl/Getty Images OpenAI's "dots" AI agents are facing an identity crisis due to name conflicts with other companies. SpaceXAI recently bought a domain name called dot.com. Internet users say the timing suggests more than a coincidence. OpenAI’s new AI agents are meant to help people get work done. Instead, their first job may be to explain that they're not a Chinese AI lab, a small fashion retailer, or Elon Musk's Grok. At its DevDay event on Tuesday, OpenAI unveiled Dots , a fleet of always-on AI assistants that can keep working across projects after a user closes the chat. In CEO Sam Altman's presentation, the agents appeared as colorful, cartoonish blob avatars. Judging by the internet’s response after the name was unveiled, OpenAI's new product name is also extremely difficult to look up. For one, it's already associated with two Chinese AI companies. Last year, social media company RedNote spun out an AI group called Dots Studio, which makes vision language models. In April 2025, another company, Shanghai Shengdongshizhang Technology, filed a US trademark application for DOTS, covering AI chatbot and personal-assistant software, making OpenAI's new agent name a particularly on-the-nose collision. Then there's Dots, which appears to be a small women's fashion company. Its Instagram page, which redirects visitors to dots.com, was quickly invaded by people who said that OpenAI's new product could accidentally send a windfall its way. “How much did open ai pay you guys?” one person asked in a comment on Instagram “Bro gonna get crazy money,” wrote another. On a separate post, commenters asked, “Is this ChatGPT?” and one optimist advised the company not to sell its domain for less than $1 million. A well-timed jab Elon Musk's SpaceXAI could also benefit from the confusion if people mistype the name. The web address dot.com sends visitors somewhere else entirely: a download page for SpaceXAI’s Grok Bot , its own AI agent system. On Tuesday, that led some X users to accuse Musk’s AI company of being an all-time petty troll. One widely shared post laid out the joke: “OpenAI just announced Dots. SpaceXAI bought Dot.com.” The post had more than 3 million views on Tuesday evening. If you look closely, you can see it pic.twitter.com/IQb7gLA5KG — Riedsschichter (@riedsschichter) September 29, 2026 However, domain ownership records show that dot.com's ownership was updated on July 28, months before OpenAI unveiled Dots. SpaceXAI has not publicly explained why it acquired the address, leaving the internet free to interpret its redirect to Grok Bot as a particularly well-timed jab at OpenAI. SpaceXAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. The internet's accusations also stem from the rivalry between the two AI companies. Musk co-founded OpenAI in 2015, left its board in 2018, and later started xAI, now part of SpaceXAI. He has also sued OpenAI and Altman over the company's move toward a for-profit structure. events.title: HSBC unveils RedCoin as name of its Hong Kong stablecoin for 3.3 million PayMe users
events.summary: A survey by the lender shows that 74 per cent of customers know at least one use case, but there are also misunderstandings HSBC on Wednesday named its stablecoin offering HSBC RedCoin, paving the way for Hong Kong’s biggest lender to make the coin available to the more than 3.3 million users of its PayMe app for money transfers, shopping and dining. When launched before the end of the year, the stablecoin would be offered only through PayMe and HSBC’s Hong Kong mobile banking app, HSBC said. The bank said it was optimistic about retail usage of HSBC RedCoin, as 74 per cent of respondents to a survey of more than 1,000 customers recognised at least one use case for stablecoins. The most recognised case, chosen by 57 per cent of respondents, was stablecoins being used for digital asset trading and tokenised investments, the survey showed. Person-to-person money transfers ranked second at 53 per cent, while cross-border remittances and merchant payments each stood at 52 per cent.

events.title: Mortgage squeeze hits Tasmanians after repeated rate rises
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tasmania's lower wages make for a uncomfortable interest rate rise As news of the latest interest rate hike sinks in, Tasmanians are assessing what it means for them. ( AAP ) Tasmanians are bracing themselves after the latest interest rate hike, with average wages lower than the mainland Australian states. Local home and business owners say they're having to find ways to absorb the additional costs. A consumer research expert is encouraging the government to look at different ways to manage inflation. Alex Gill and her partner built their family home in Tasmania's south three years ago. Like a lot of new builds, it ended up costing the family more than they'd budgeted for. The latest interest rate rise will make things tighter for the family of four. Tasmanian homeowner Alex Gill says the repeated interest rate rises are definitely having an impact. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) The Reserve Bank increases interest rates to 4.6 per cent in its fourth rate rise this year. Ms Gill said she may have to consider increasing her part-time working hours. And while on average Tasmania's wages are on average lower than other states, Ms Gill said the family have no plans to move interstate. "We're just going to have to make it work because we love being here, we love Tasmania," she said. But, if interest rates continue to climb, the family may need to consider more drastic action. Tasmanian homeowner Ella Tenni is in the process of buying and selling at the moment, and says the interest rate rise does add some uncertainty into the mix. ( ABC News: Kate Nickels ) Ella Tenni, who also lives in Southern Tasmania, is weighing up what the interest rate rise will mean for her family. "We're in the process of selling and buying at the moment," Ms Tenni said. "So I did have a bit of a pause, maybe feeling a bit worried about that, but in the scheme of things we're in a position that we'll be able to absorb it." She said she sometimes worries about further interest rate rises. "But then I do sometimes put my head in the sand and try not to think about it." The average new loan size for Tasmania at the start of the year was $505,000. ( ABC News: Jacinta Bos ) Consumer research company Canstar has looked at what impact the 0.25 per cent cash rate hike will have on monthly mortgage repayments. What's impacted in the RBA rate hike While the RBA's decisions are most felt through mortgage repayments, their impact extends well beyond home loans. For someone who took out the average new loan size for Tasmania at the start of the year of $505,000, the rate hike will translate into an increase to their minimum monthly repayments of $81. That's based on a 30-year loan at a variable rate of 5.50 per cent. "While plenty of households might be able to handle this kind of increase in isolation, across what has now been four cash rate hikes in 2026, that same borrower has seen their monthly repayments rise by a total of $322," Canstar's Sally Tindall said. Sally Tindall says the repeat rate rises are having a compounding impact on households across the country. ( Supplied: CANSTAR ) On top of that, Tasmania's wages are the lowest in the country. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, Tasmania's average weekly earnings are $1846.30 — compared with a national figure of $2083.70. The latest figures from Cotality show the median property value in Hobart is over $750 000, while still cheaper than most states and territories, it has been on the rise since the pandemic. Businesses bracing for belt-tightening Andrew Turner says the topic of inflation and rate rises is on the minds of customers and staff alike. ( ABC News: Mackenzie Heard ) Andrew Turner owns a café and brewery in Burnie. He said every time interest rates rise, there's a change in sentiment among his customers. "I don't know if we get a huge drop in revenue, but it's definitely something everyone is talking about," he said. Andrew Turner says he's expecting customers to keep tightening their belt, due to the cost of living. ( ABC Northern Tasmania: Monte Bovill ) "Even our staff are talking about now having issues affording their homes." He said he's expecting future rate rises will start to affect customer spending and his business won't be in a position to drop prices. "All of our costs have gone through the roof as well, and now with the surcharge ban we're looking at absorbing a significant cost as a part of that." Tips for mortgage holders and advice for government Canstar's Sally Tindall said it was time the government considered looking at a different way to manage inflation, other than the RBA lifting interest rates.

events.title: Apple Pay finally launches in India after years on the sidelines
events.summary: Last day to demo your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Apple began rolling out Apple Pay in India on Tuesday, as TechCrunch was first to report. Its first banking partner is Axis Bank, the country’s third-largest private-sector lender. The move brings the company’s payments service to the world’s most populous country after years of delays in a market dominated by the state-backed United Payments Interface (UPI). The initial rollout is limited. Apple Pay supports eligible Axis Bank cards on Visa and Mastercard, but not India’s homegrown RuPay network. Acceptance will also be restricted to merchants and payment terminals that have been enabled for the service. Apple said the service would be accepted by “millions of merchants” across India, including Blinkit, Croma, Ixigo, Reliance brands, Tata 1mg, and Zomato. The company has worked with payment service providers including Cashfree, JusPay, Mswipe, Paytm, PayU, Pine Labs, Razorpay, and Worldline to enable Apple Pay acceptance. Unlike India’s ubiquitous Unified Payments Interface (UPI) system, which lets consumers make instant bank-to-bank payments without relying on cards, Apple Pay is card-based and requires individual issuers and payment infrastructure providers to integrate with the service. This makes a broad rollout more complex. Apple’s commercial terms have also emerged as a sticking point with some of India’s largest banks, the people said. Apple is seeking a fee of about 20 basis points (0.2%) on transactions, according to the people, a significant bite out of the roughly 40 to 50 basis points (0.4% to 0.5%) of margin in the payments layer. The fee structure is broadly consistent with Apple Pay’s commercial model in other markets, the people said. HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and SBI Card are not supporting Apple Pay at launch as negotiations over commercial terms continue, one of the people told TechCrunch. Apple, Axis Bank, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and SBI Card did not respond to requests for comment on the launch. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that Apple was preparing to launch Apple Pay in India in October, starting with Axis Bank credit cards. Apple Pay has entered a payments market that looks markedly different from the U.S. and other card-heavy economies. India’s digital payments boom has been driven largely by UPI, the state-backed system that lets consumers move money directly between bank accounts. UPI handles the bulk of digital payments in India, where scanning a QR code to pay directly from a bank account has become commonplace. Apple Pay, by contrast, initially addresses a much smaller card payments market. Nevertheless, Apple Pay could appeal to India’s growing base of iPhone users, who tend to be more affluent and are more likely to use premium credit cards. Those customers could make the service hard for banks to ignore, despite UPI’s dominance. Even if Apple Pay remains a niche service, the economics could still make India meaningful for Apple. The transaction fee the iPhone maker would charge would give it another way to monetize its growing base of iPhone users in the country, the people said. At launch, eligible Axis Bank customers can add their credit cards to Apple’s Wallet app and use Apple Pay for online purchases as well as contactless payments at supported terminals, the people said. An Apple Pay transaction could work at a terminal operated by an independent payments provider that has enabled the service but fail at another terminal whose acquiring bank has not, one of the people said. That could make acceptance uneven during the initial rollout, even for customers with supported cards. The launch adds another piece to Apple’s growing business in India, where it has been expanding iPhone sales, local manufacturing, and its retail footprint. Apple accounted for 28% of India’s smartphone market by value in 2025, up from 23% a year earlier, per an earlier report by Counterpoint Research. India already accounts for about a quarter of global iPhone production , and that share could rise to 30% to 35% over the next five years, Indian English daily Business Standard reported last month, citing an Indian government official. events.title: Crystal Jade holding companies in S’pore, Hong Kong placed under receivership
events.summary: The group has about 13 outlets in operation here, as listed on its website. SINGAPORE – The holding companies of restaurant group Crystal Jade’s operations in Singapore and Hong Kong have been placed under receivership, with advisory firm Kroll reviewing the group’s financial and operational affairs. Receivership generally involves an independent party being appointed to take control of some or all of a company’s assets, typically when it is unable to meet its financial obligations. Kroll said on Sept 30 that its representatives have been appointed as receivers over Singapore-incorporated Crystal Jade Culinary Concepts Holding and Hong Kong-incorporated Crystal Jade Culinary Concepts Holding (Great China). “The representatives are undertaking a review of the group’s financial and operational affairs, including assessing strategic options available for its portfolio of brands, restaurants and businesses with a view to stabilise the business and preserve value,” said Kroll. “Stakeholders will be engaged regarding potential restructuring as and when appropriate.” Crystal Jade’s current shareholders include entities by Affirma Capital and L Capital Asia, which is the Asian private equity arm backed by luxury conglomerate LVMH. ST understands that the receivership is part of a process to facilitate L Capital Asia’s eventual exit from Crystal Jade, though it is unclear why receivership was chosen as part of the exit process. In Singapore, the group recently closed its outlets at The Clementi Mall, Jurong Point and Great World, bringing the home-grown Chinese restaurant group’s total number of shuttered outlets in 2026 to five. One of its entities, Crystal Jade Fine Dining, was recently charged for failing to submit its complete income tax return on time without a reasonable excuse, which is an offence under the Income Tax Act. Kroll added that key members of Crystal Jade’s management team will continue to oversee the group’s restaurant operations. In response to queries from The Straits Times, the Kroll representatives confirmed that “it is not a closure of the business, and Crystal Jade is not exiting the food and beverage market”. Similarly, a Crystal Jade spokesperson told ST that “customers can continue to enjoy the same quality, service and dining experience at Crystal Jade restaurants”. “Throughout this period, the group remains committed to ensuring smooth continuity of service to its customers, while preserving Crystal Jade’s brand and its value,” he added. When ST visited Crystal Jade’s Takashimaya outlet just after 2pm on Sept 30, diners were seen having lunch as usual. Staff at the outlet said it was expected to remain open, but did not provide further details. One diner, who declined to be named, said she was there for the restaurant’s 35 per cent off “tea-time special” and had not visited in some time. She said the news of the receivership did not affect her view of the restaurant, adding that she would return if the promotion continued.

events.title: Three takeaways from Trump's 'Super Intelligence' summit
events.summary: Trump met top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday to discuss AI Published 30 September 2026, 03:41 BST US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age". The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry. The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity. Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House. Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting. The president said the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks. Under the agreement, which Trump posted online , external , the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology. The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues. They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways." The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. "It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president." Trump with top tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board. Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended, calling the meeting a "historic conversation". Amodei called it a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins". But not all technology experts are impressed with the accord. Nanyang Technological University AI governance researcher Jose Miguelito Enriquez said the pact shows "emerging consensus" but does not address whether AI developers should be held accountable for incidents. It is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations around the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatherall from the University of Sydney. The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are for any breaches, Weatherall said. "The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added. Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings Published 16 September Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? Published 17 September Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks in response to calls from some industry figures for tighter oversight over the technology. On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model , GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns. The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation . Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards". The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added. Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI. The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the US over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on communities. Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November. A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News , external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas. Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres. "These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters. The president previously said on social media that the only reason communities should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor".
