events.title: Why passengers are being barred from rear carriages on these Sydney trains
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Back carriages on Tangara train services shut for school holidays amid security breaches People have been spotted riding on the back of Tangara trains, prompting a crackdown. ( Supplied: NSW Government ) Frequent incidents of train surfing and vandalism have prompted a security crackdown on Tangara trains, with rear carriages to be shut throughout the NSW school holiday period. The lack of CCTV on the trains has made them susceptible to vandalism, as has the "buffer": a platform at the rear from which train surfers can jump from the platform. Only one out of 55 Tangara trains has been refurbished two years on from a state government pledge to upgrade the aging fleet and install CCTV. Passengers are being barred from using the rear carriages of all Tangara trains to prevent people breaking into the crew cabs and riding on the back of them. The policy was already in force on selected night-time and weekend services, but has now been applied to every Tangara train for the duration of the school holidays. More than two years have passed since the government announced a $447 million program to improve security and extend the life of the aging Tangara fleet by up to 12 years. To date, only one out of 55 Tangara trains has received the full refurbishment, including a CCTV system. It means passengers, including those travelling on grand final weekend, will find the rear carriages of Tangaras locked and the lights turned off. The lights will be switched off and the doors locked on the back carriages. ( ABC News: Taryn Southcombe ) 'Commuters first, dropkicks second' Shadow NSW Transport Minister Natalie Ward said it was "embarrassing" the government had effectively surrendered to vandals and train-surfers. "It can't be 'lights out' for commuters. You can't give up on this," she said. "Transport policy has to be commuters first, dropkicks second." However, state Transport Minister John Graham said misbehaviour on trains risked derailing the schedule, causing more inconvenience for commuters in the long run. He said locking up the rear carriages was a "pragmatic step". "It's one we don't want to take, but reliability is our number one focus." A covering has been installed to prevent people from train surfing. ( Supplied: NSW Government ) Train-surfing or "buffer riding" has been an ongoing issue on the Tangaras, fuelled by social media videos where people post and boast about their "achievements". The lack of CCTV on the fleet has made the trains especially susceptible to vandalism, as has the "buffer": a platform at the rear of the Tangaras from which train surfers can jump from the platform. To eliminate the dangerous practice, Sydney Trains fitted slanted "nose cones" onto all the buffers, to deprive train surfers of a flat surface. On the T4 Eastern Suburbs and Illawarra line, there were only three incidents between July and September, whereas there were 127 cases of buffer riding in the 12 months prior. "Those cones have made a big difference," Mr Graham said. The nose cones have had some success in reducing incidents of train surfing. ( Supplied: NSW Government ) However, Rail, Tram and Bus Union secretary Toby Warnes said the internal door to the crew cab was being repeatedly targeted. "I've seen some of the social media videos myself," he said. "It doesn't take much to open that. And once you have opened that, it's not then difficult to open the actual door to get out onto the [rear] platform." He said people hoping to "big note" themselves were risking their own lives, and the safety of others. "It puts the people who are operating the train in danger and the general public too, particularly if it's being done near stations," he said. Internal Sydney Trains documents seen by the ABC suggest the organisation is scrambling to install new locks on crew cab doors. Plain-clothes security officers are also patrolling some Tangara trains. The lack of CCTV in the Tangaras makes them vulnerable to vandalism. ( ABC News ) The once-futuristic Tangara was introduced in 1988 and will remain in service until the mid 2030s, while a replacement is built. The Minns government plans to build the new fleet in the Hunter, where the Tangara was manufactured, thanks to a $12 billion investment over 15 years. Chris Minns's government is overseeing the refurbishment of the Tangara fleet. ( ABC News ) However, the state opposition has criticised the speed of the Tangara refurbishment program, which includes computer, security and customer information system upgrades. Ms Ward said the $447 million program had only refurbished a single train since it was announced in June 2024.

events.title: Supreme Court green-lights Trump's third-country deportations
events.summary: The Supreme Court will allow the Trump administration to resume rapidly deporting immigrants to "third countries" and will consider the legal question at a later date. The big picture: The policy of expelling migrants to countries that are not their home country has faced legal challenges from early in the president's second term — and the Supreme Court has once again cleared the administration's way. Driving the news: The court stayed a February 2026 order that detained immigrants should have "the right to meaningful notice" and should be able to raise concerns before being deported to a third country. The three liberal justices would have denied the administration's application for a stay. That prior order from U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy, much of which was backed by a recent appeals court decision, said the administration's policy "fails to satisfy due process for a raft of reasons." This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: Trump, Johnson preview a new AI self-policing pact
events.summary: President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters today that they’re preparing to release a self-regulatory accord with AI frontier labs. The still-unreleased pact raises questions about enforcement — Johnson referred to “consequences” for AI companies that fall short — and the depth of oversight. Trump summed up his approach to AI safety by telling Semafor’s White House correspondent that “there should be tremendous self-regulation” after a White House meeting with more than a dozen AI and tech CEOs, but Johnson billed the forthcoming industry pact as “robust internal controls and layers of internal and external review.” He added that “Congress is going to keep steady hands at the wheel on this. We’ll continue to assess and further deliberate in the days ahead.” Trump and Johnson lunched with the executives as the administration unveiled a new AI-powered site, America.gov , that’s aimed at providing easier access to government services. Trump also told reporters after the meeting that the Justice Department and FBI would handle any regulatory issues with AI and that he’d be signing an executive order today that replaces “artificial intelligence” with “superintelligence” in governmental communications. He praised data centers, saying they have made communities very rich. Trump’s laudatory comments come as bipartisan angst over the technology crests, alarming AI incidents proliferate, and global governments call for policy cooperation. — Ashley Gold and Shelby Talcott

events.title: Prediction market traders think the U.S. added more jobs in September than economists estimate
events.summary: Traders on prediction market platform Kalshi think there's almost 60% odds that the U.S. added more than 90,000 payrolls in September, and also place a 50-50 chance that it generated more than 100,000 jobs. That's higher than economists surveyed by Dow Jones' consensus estimate for 84,000 jobs made in the month. The September jobs report is set to be delivered by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Friday. Prediction market traders are expecting another strong jobs report on Friday. Following August's bigger-than-expected employment report — where the U.S. added 162,000 jobs during the month — traders on prediction market platform Kalshi think there's a 60% chance the country added more than 90,000 jobs during September. Speculators also think there's almost 50-50 odds that the report is once again in six figures. That's higher than the Dow Jones consensus economist consensus forecast of 84,000. On the contracts, traders are asked whether they think the U.S. added more than a certain number of jobs in the month. The market and its contracts are resolved using official data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Traders on Polymarket also think there's about 50-50 odds the September jobs report is in the six figure range. The contracts on Polymarket are resolved the same way as on Kalshi. While the labor market earlier in the summer showed signs of weakness , August's jobs report showed it rebounding. It also gave monetary policymakers at the Federal Reserve greater cover to focus on its inflation mandate, which remains above target , and raise interest rates at its September meeting. The September employment report is set to be delivered on Friday at 8:30 a.m. Before that, ADP's national employment report will be released on Wednesday at 8:15 a.m. ET. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: Alaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel race
events.summary: Alaska Airlines is overhauling its Alaska and Hawaiian cabins to include brand-new top-tier suites, a premium-economy class and other features. The overhaul comes amid an industrywide investment to add more higher-priced seats. Hawaiian and Alaska completed their merger in September 2024 but will continue to operate as distinct brands. Alaska Airlines is overhauling cabins across Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines to add hundreds of high-end seats and building new airport lounges, banking on customers' continued willingness to pay a premium for travel luxuries to grow its profits into the next decade. The changes were announced ahead of Alaska's investor day in Seattle on Tuesday, when the carrier's executives will face questions on the new offerings, how the airline is coping with the profit-eating surge in jet fuel this year, and its ability to reach its goal of $1 billion in added profit from end of 2024 to the end of 2027. It said Tuesday that it's two-thirds of the way there. Investors are also likely to tie the new products to the company's prospects to grow its co-branded credit card and loyalty program, which have generated billions for airlines. Alaska said it's working to become more reliant on revenue from premium seats, international flights, its loyalty program and cargo, which is higher margin than the main cabin. It forecast on Tuesday that those more lucrative products will reach close to 60% of its total revenue by 2030, up from 53% currently. Even with the cabin changes, Alaska, which completed its merger with Hawaiian Airlines in September 2024, will continue to operate the two airlines as separate brands. Alaska's Boeing 787 Dreamliners will get 34 lie-flat suites in a new offering it's calling Aurora. It will also have 35 seats in a new premium-economy section, called Premium Reserve, on the 787-9 and 787-10, starting in 2028. "At least" 25 of the yet-to-be certified Boeing 737 Max 10s will have 12 lie-flat Aurora suites and premium-economy seats, a bid to compete with other airlines on lucrative cross-country routes. Hawaiian Airlines' 24 Airbus A330s will each get 22 all-new first-class suites with sliding doors, starting in 2028, and its first-ever premium-economy section, with 28 seats. The carrier will open a new 41,000-square-foot Alaska lounge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, with dedicated space for Aurora suites flyers, similar to the tiered lounge system Delta Air Lines , United Airlines and American Airlines have. Hawaiian is building an almost 13,000-square-foot lounge in Honolulu's Terminal 1, slated to open in early 2028. U.S. airlines have been spending the past few years revamping their cabins to add more premium seats, often at the expense of coach seats, since first-class fares can go for many times more than an economy-class ticket, and customers keep paying to sit closer to the front. Most of Alaska Airlines' fleet doesn't have lie-flat or other premium options that are common on competitors' jets. Alaska is far from the first carrier to remodel its cabins, but that might work to its benefit when the fresh product hits the market. "There is an advantage to being the last mover in that you've seen what your competitors have and if you want to you can try to one-up them," said Henry Harteveldt, founder of Atmosphere Research Group, a travel consulting firm. The Hawaiian Airlines Airbus A330s, used for flights to Hawaii, Asia and Oceania, have "aging interiors," said Shane Jones, Alaska's head of fleet. The new options will bring the total count down to 254 seats from 278 on those planes. Jones said the new options will give Hawaiian a range of premium choices, from the honeymoon splurge to repeat Hawaii visitors looking for a step-up from coach. He told CNBC that the airline spent months looking at fabric samples at the company's headquarters in Seattle under different types of lighting to pick the right one. Some shades were too bright pink, while others were too drab. He said that the airline wanted to evoke the colors and mood of tropical escapes to Hawaii with a wave pattern sewn into the seat, and that the carrier evaluated how many waves were enough because too many could be dizzying. Hawaiian Airlines CEO Diana Birkett Rakow said more than half of Hawaii's visitors are traveling from the West Coast of the U.S., a customer base that is "valuable to us from an economic perspective, just in terms of their income, their travel budget, their spending patterns, their flying patterns. And so this gives us an opportunity to elevate the experience." Meanwhile, Alaska has been expanding its international flying from Seattle, including to London, Iceland and Italy, with more destinations slated to begin this fall. International travel demand has held up despite surging fuel prices, airline executives have said.

events.title: Two Indian nationals charged with smuggling counterfeit Ozempic from China: DOJ
events.summary: Two Indian nationals were charged in Florida federal court with allegedly smuggling counterfeit Ozempic from China, the DOJ said. The scheme purportedly continued even after the FDA seized some of the fake weight-loss drugs in 2023 and warned the public about it. Swapnadip Roy was extradited from Italy and made his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in Tampa, Florida, in the case. Roy is charged with Vicky Ramancha. Two Indian nationals have been charged in federal court in Florida with an alleged conspiracy to smuggle counterfeit Ozempic from China in a scheme that purportedly continued even after the Food and Drug Administration seized some of the fake weight-loss drugs in 2023 and warned the public about it, the Department of Justice said Tuesday. One of the men, 33-year-old Swapnadip Roy, was extradited from Italy and made his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday. Roy and his alleged co-conspirator, Vicky Ramancha, 37, are charged in an indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit smuggling and to defraud the U.S., three counts of smuggling, and two counts of selling counterfeit drugs and holding counterfeit drugs for sale. If convicted, they both face a maximum sentence of 71 years in prison. Trump holds up to $1 billion in bonds tied to institutions he can affect Rep. James Comer expands House investigation into prediction market insider trading Hassett: 'We're still working our way out from' Biden Covid spending Court documents state Roy and Ramancha, starting in July 2023 and continuing to the following April, allegedly obtained counterfeit Ozempic from unauthorized sources in China. The popular drug is made by Novo , which recently rebranded from its name Novo Nordisk. The material they and their co-conspirators allegedly distributed "included counterfeit packaging, package inserts, pen labels, and needles meant to deceive downstream customers into believing they were purchasing authentic Ozempic authorized by the manufacturer," DOJ said. The newly unsealed indictment says that in July 2023, Ramancha executed a sales and purchase agreement with an unidentified company in Lakeland, Florida, agreeing to supply that company with a product described as being Ozempic "at deeply discounted pricing." A month later, Ramancha executed another agreement with a company in Sanford, Florida, to supply it with a product described as "Ozempic syringes" at deeply discounted pricing, the indictment alleges. in November 2023, "Roy utilized threats to facilitate the distribution of product in the United States," writing, "Listen i am not your friend okay? I am not that guy," the indictment alleges. Roy continued, "I am the guy that will cut some one [expletive] head off and [expletive] peoples dead wives corpse with it," the indictment alleges. "You [expletive] up Solve the [expletive] problem. Get the truck over there today." After Roy and Ramancha learned that the FDA had seized some of their product that they had distributed in the U.S., a co-conspirator asked Ramancha whether the related FDA warning would affect a pending order to 60,000 additional units of Ozempic, the indictment says. "Ramancha replied, 'Not at all. But you have to make sure your client are not being idiotic,'" the indictment alleges. The case comes as the use of so-called GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic for weight loss has become increasingly popular in the U.S. In July, Gallup reported that the percentage of U.S. adults who take GLP-1 medications for weight loss purposes rose to 11% in 2026, compared to 3% in 2024. "And 15% report having used the medicine for weight loss at some point, an increase of nine percentage points" over 2024, Gallup noted. "Counterfeit prescription drugs — especially common ones — threaten the health and safety of every American who depends on the integrity of our pharmaceutical supply," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ's Criminal Division said in a statement Tuesday. "These defendants allegedly exploited people's health to pay themselves. We will keep pursuing anyone who seeks to deceive American consumers with counterfeit drugs," Duva said.

events.title: OpenAI’s latest features take direct aim at the app store model
events.summary: Last day to demo your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. The focus of OpenAI’s Dev Day on Tuesday may have been on its agentic assistants known as Dots , or its new AI models , but combined, the AI company’s announcements pointed towards a bigger plan: a disruption of the traditional app store model. Taken together, today’s announcements turn ChatGPT itself into the place where software can be discovered, launched, and used by people and agents alike. In addition, OpenAI introduced a way for people to bring their ChatGPT identity with them, while also allowing them to use their existing AI allowance in third-party apps. This isn’t the first time OpenAI has experimented with how apps could operate within its familiar chatbot interface, but the current vision feels more fleshed out than before. For starters, the company is turning ChatGPT itself into a surface for launching apps. The chatbot, which the company says now has 1.2 billion weekly users, has yet to fully capitalize on its potential as a discovery mechanism for finding and using apps that work with AI. To change that, ChatGPT will begin to make app suggestions within the flow of conversation when it recognizes that a particular app could help the user complete their task. From there, the user will be able to connect the app and begin using it directly within ChatGPT. This is also aided by the expansion of ChatGPT’s plugin architecture, which now supports extensions. This allows app developers to build interactive panels where users can work with their tools while they’re chatting with ChatGPT. This essentially turns the apps and services that users would have previously used via the web or through a native desktop or mobile app into something that’s operated directly within ChatGPT. Developers that sign on with the system can build AI-native versions of their apps through ChatGPT, the same way they would through the open web or a mobile app store. As more and more discovery happens through AI chat, it’s a distribution channel that’s hard to pass up. Users get an incentive to use that channel too, because “ Sign in with ChatGPT ” will let them bring their AI allowance with them. (OpenAI has 16 launch partners on this effort, including Cognition’s Devin, Notion, Vercel, T3, OpenClaw, and Dactyl, but plans to add more soon, it says.) In a demo at OpenAI’s Dev Day event, the company showed off how its own new meeting app could work inside ChatGPT, showing upcoming meetings from the user’s calendar. Here, the user could easily choose to use AI to take meeting notes, then receive a summary of follow-up items when the meeting wrapped. In another example, users would work with design-focused apps like those from Figma and Adobe to work on revisions of their current project or use a particular feature that would have otherwise required a standalone app. The apps can be shared with others, like work colleagues, in the lightweight websites ChatGPT now produces. From these ChatGPT sites, a user’s coworkers could sign in to the app with their own credentials and permissions, making the software experience personalized to them. OpenAI also talked about improvements to how developers submit plugins for review — OpenAI’s version of Apple’s App Review process, if you will. Now, developers will be able to track their review, see what needs to be fixed, request a human review, and update their plugin’s tools without starting their whole submission over. The company also announced a new enterprise app marketplace where partners can market their services. At launch, there are some 30-plus partners offering their app through the OpenAI Marketplace, including Adobe, Figma, Sierra, Decagon, HubSpot, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Harvey, Legora, Palo Alto Networks, CrowdStrike, Baseten, and others. Eligible customers can apply part of their OpenAI commitment toward approved partner software, OpenAI said. Beyond turning ChatGPT into an app discovery tool where users connect with apps directly, OpenAI’s embrace of agents is gently pushing users into a new era where they don’t have to think as much about which app to use or why, relying instead on their AI agents’ suggestions. With the launch of its autonomous AI agents known as Dots , agents will navigate the web for you, executing the tasks that need to be done in their own cloud infrastructure. Each Dot has its own cloud computer and browser, and can also use connected apps. Compare this to the old model, where users who wanted to manage some type of project — like building a website or coordinating a meeting calendar — would have to download different apps to their computer or phone to make that happen. Now, users will instead tell an AI agent what they want to have done, and it will simply do it for them.

events.title: Cafe owner faces costly legal battle as retail laws gather dust
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Cafe faces costly court case to settle landlord dispute as retail laws passed four years ago still not enacted Hayley Dick has run her own cafe in George Town in Tasmania's north for 18 months. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) A small business owner is facing a $50,000 legal bill to settle a lease dispute as new Tasmanian laws have not come into effect. An overhaul of the state's retail laws passed parliament four years ago. The government says amendments are needed before enacting the "complex" act. It has been four years since the Tasmanian government overhauled the state's retail laws, with one of its aims to help small business owners resolve disputes without going to court. But that has been no comfort for cafe owner Hayley Dick. Despite the act passing parliament and receiving royal assent from the governor, only two of the 90 sections have come into effect. It has left Ms Dick locked in a months-long dispute with her landlord over responsibility for a compliance issue: the installation of a grease trap. It is a dispute that may end up in the courts. Hayley Dick has written to state politicians for help. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) The Retail Leases Act 2022 reformed the Fair Trading retail laws and regulations legislated in 1998. The laws relate to the rights and obligations of landlords and tenants of those in retail or other business premises. The Department of Justice says when commenced, the new act will provide powers for a prescribed body to make determinations in relation to certain matters for retail tenancy disputes. In the meantime, Ms Dick says there are limited resources to help with her dispute. Hayley Dick says it has been a frustrating and stressful year dealing with the dispute. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) She is currently in discussion with lawyers to escalate the issue to court and estimates she may face hefty legal costs. "Why is it that we don't have anywhere to go to?" Last year, Ms Dick took over the lease of a cafe premises in George Town, in the state's north. A letter from TasWater to the building's owners in February, seen by the ABC, states the building will become non-compliant from August if a 1,000-kilogram grease trap is not installed. A grease trap or arrester acts like a strainer to catch food waste in wastewater. A grease trap keeps food scraps and other by-products out of wastewater. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) The owners passed the notice to Ms Dick, who says the alteration would cost at least $29,000 But Ms Dick's lease strictly states she is not to alter the structure of the premises. She believes the responsibility of installing the trap sits with the building's owners. "Because they keep saying they're not taking responsibility, we have nowhere to go but to the Supreme Court or another court to actually get a ruling on it to be able to get them to do it," Ms Dick said. TasWater is urging the business owners to install a "compliant liquid trade waste pre-treatment system" at the premises. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) The landlords were contacted for comment but did not respond to questioning. Instead, they referred the ABC to other lease and business bodies such as The Real Estate Institute of Tasmania (REIT) or Tenant's Union of Tasmania. Small Business Minister Guy Barnett responded to Ms Dick's unanswered emails after the ABC began making enquiries. "Although other legislative priorities have affected the timing of this reform, I want to assure you that work to implement the Retail Leases Act 2022 is continuing," he wrote to Ms Dick. "I recognise that court proceedings can be costly and time-consuming, particularly for small businesses." Ms Dick said she had spent about $5,000 on legal fees. Hayley Dick is not sure where to turn to resolve the dispute. ( ABC News: Kelsey Reid ) Responding to ABC questions, Mr Barnett said the government was committed to implementing the act and its mediation arrangements. "With feedback from a number of stakeholders identifying that further amendments were required and a commitment was made to the Legislative Council to bring the bill back to parliament before it is proclaimed [enacted]," he said. "Retail tenancy disputes remain subject to the existing Retail Tenancies Code, and CBOS (Consumer Building and Occupational Services) can assist parties to resolve disputes, including through investigation and negotiation." Guy Barnett says the act needs to go back to parliament for amendments.

events.title: Trump launches America.gov with AI chatbots at its core
events.summary: If you want accurate information about life-changing government services, a potentially hallucinating chatbot might not be your first choice. However, the Trump administration is rolling out a new digital portal for access to federal government tasks that puts AI front and center, even though there are concerns that existing federal digital services may be in danger. Trump announced the launch of America.gov in an executive order on Tuesday, describing the new site as a “unified digital front door to the Federal Government for every individual in the US seeking Federal information or services.” As to what that front door will look like, the key thing to pay attention to in the EO is that the site is a place to “communicate in plain language” and ostensibly “receive accurate answers,” and we all know what that means: It’s an AI chatbot. Google confirmed as much in its own announcement that it was a technology partner in the America.gov initiative, "leveraging Gemini to help more than 100 million people access critical public resources with greater speed and ease.” A White House spokesperson told The Register that xAI’s Grok is the other tech partner on the initiative, so watch out for vulgar responses when you ask a simple question. “Advances in technology now make possible a fundamentally different relationship between the people and the Federal Government,” Trump’s EO read in part. It says individuals will be able to “where authorized and technically available, complete Government transactions without being required to navigate the websites of multiple agencies.” Navigate to the site right now and you’re met with a messy site that the National Design Studio, which claims responsibility for its layout, ought to be ashamed of. A paragraph summarizing the purpose of the site is interspersed with graphics that serve no purpose and only interfere with the flow of the text, including one mimicking the fingerprint icon from iOS that actually overlaps with the words before and after it. Scroll down to see some of the tasks that the site claims it will be able to handle, like comparing medication costs, updating your legal name across multiple agencies, or submitting a passport application, and clicking on every single one of them only shows that the feature is coming sometime in 2027. The White House tells us that the embedded chatbots can provide complete answers culled from the 29,000 government websites that were ingested for the platform, but all those additional features will be coming over time. What you have now on America.gov, then, is just a federal government chatbot powered by Gemini and Grok that refers users to other websites - helpful, but not exactly the central portal Trump promised in his EO. The Office of Management and Budget has 90 days to tell agencies how they're supposed to implement their integration with America.gov, meaning it could be a while before the site is as useful as the administration promises, if it ever is at all. In the meantime, it gives Google and xAI a rather high-profile proving ground for their chatbots, courtesy of the federal government. America.gov’s privacy policy claims that the project’s tech partners are operating under zero data retention agreements, so user prompts and responses aren’t retained, sold, turned into advertising profiles, or used to train their AIs. The White House further asserted to us that no user messages are transmitted to Gemini or Grok, though the privacy policy also mentions that America.gov’s AI providers may be sent approximate area information to make results more relevant, which seems to contradict the White House’s claim. Digital service reliability in doubt The idea that the Trump administration would put access to the federal government behind AI chatbots isn’t surprising given how readily the White House has embraced AI since Trump returned to office. A recent coup at the team overseeing the US Web Design System, which maintains design standards and provides components that help government websites from the federal all the way down to the local level meet accessibility requirements, has furthered the AI push as well. As reported last week by FedScoop, the decade-old USWDS was recently purged of its leadership, putting a self-described AI engineer from the Treasury Department in charge of the system. The new USWDS chief, Ryan Parker, said that he plans to automate as much accessibility testing as possible across the system. The state of the system has led a group of current and former government web design leaders and contributors to the open-source USWDS to sound the alarm in an open letter to the General Services Administration that, coincidentally or not, was published, again by FedScoop, not long before the America.gov announcement. With the Trump administration seemingly set on placing as many government services as it can within reach of an AI chatbot that could make critical mistakes, open and accessible web services available elsewhere from the government remain essential. If the open letter's concerns prove well founded, those services could become less reliable, but hey - at least you’ll be able to chat to Grok about it on America.gov without any way to actually solve your problem until sometime in 2027. ®

events.title: Inside the fossil fuel industry's push into Australian classrooms
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Fossil fuel giants behind hundreds of programs targeting Australian children Fossil fuel companies spend millions on a range of science programs and teaching resources. ( Supplied: CommsDeclare/Glencore Coal ) A teaching schedule was disrupted and students were invited to "drill for oil" by an industry-backed education program sponsored by major fossil fuel companies. A recent investigation found oil and gas companies have spent tens of millions of dollars on educational partnerships. There are calls for greater scrutiny of industry-backed material and corporate influence in schools. Alison Holt had never heard of the Energy Club before she was told they would be taking over her science class. At the time, she was teaching at Busselton Senior High School in Western Australia when she realised the series of incursions would disrupt her teaching schedule. "I was told probably a day or two before because, you know, you've got to plan ahead very tightly being a science teacher," Ms Holt said. "Without any consultation and any permission from the parents, we had three hours taken out of our very tight curriculum time. "So that's nearly a week of science gone." Former Busselton Senior High School teacher Alison Holt. ( Supplied: Alison Holt ) Ms Holt recalled asking her head of department about what the program involved. "They said: 'Oh, they just come in and, you know, talk about mining and, you know, the petrochemical industry,' and immediately my hair went up on the back of my neck." Until 2021, the not-for-profit Energy Club WA used to be called The Petroleum Club of WA, and the initiative offered at Alison Holt's school was its Next Generation Energy Program, which has been running since 1991. Woodside Energy and Exxon Mobil are just two of the major oil and gas companies the Energy Club lists as sponsors. The course involves industry professionals volunteering time to deliver three lessons with a focus on "energy literacy" and career opportunities. "We invite our valued sponsors to leverage the Next Generation Schools Program," its flyer states. "By supporting our established initiative, you can maximise impact by pooling resources … save on development costs, and strengthen community ties through our well-connected framework." A presentation about natural gas is part of the Next Generation Energy Program. ( Supplied: Energy Club WA ) In March 2021, the non-profit decided "to rebrand and move forward as Energy Club WA so that the brand reflects the continued promise of connecting people with energy for a sustainable future". But as the incursion got underway at the Busselton school, Ms Holt said what she observed seemed inconsistent with that message. In one activity, the presenters used bread, chocolate spread and sprinkles to simulate how exploration drilling works. "He'd put Nutella on one piece of bread, then he'd put sprinkles on the next piece, and he'd just make this big four- or five-layer sandwich," she explained. Students were then invited up to "drill for oil" using plastic straws pushed down through the layers of bread. A chemical engineer from BP delivering the Next Generation Energy Program at a school in 2023. ( Facebook: Armadale Senior High School ) Ms Holt also had concerns about the way the presentations framed the role of gas. "He spoke about … the different sectors where energy was needed, how it was provided, and then talked about how gas was the answer, you know, in the transition to renewable energy," she said. After the first of the three sessions, Ms Holt asked whether renewable energy would also be part of the program. In a statement, Energy Club WA general manager Kate McCarthy said its educational program was reviewed by participating schools to ensure the content was appropriate. "The classroom teacher is always present during the presentation, and the teacher and school are engaged for feedback on the program and its contents at each visit," she said. According to the annual report, more than 1,800 students participated in the Next Generation Energy Program in 2025. ( Supplied: Energy Club WA ) Mentors for the program were a mix of volunteers and those still working in the industry. "Sponsors of the Next Generation schools program do not contribute to the committee to develop or review the contents of the program," Ms McCarthy said. "Energy Club WA has 20 participating schools for 2026." Design your own carbon capture solution The Energy Club was one of at least 260 educational programs in Australia sponsored by fossil fuel companies identified in a report by climate advocacy group Comms Declare.

events.title: 30-year Treasury bond yield scales to highest level since 2002
events.summary: The yields on longer-dated U.S. Treasurys rose Tuesday, adding to their rip-roaring moves to multi-year highs due to concerns around inflation and central bank monetary policy. The 30-year Treasury bond yield, which typically reacts to geopolitical developments, was more than 2 basis points higher at 5.585%. Earlier in the session, it jumped to just above 5.6%, or its highest level since June 2002 when the long-dated bond yield hit 5.644%. The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield — the key benchmark for mortgage borrowing, auto loans and credit card debt — traded about 1 basis point higher at 5.253%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which tends to move in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, fell more than 3 basis points to 4.891%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. "Investors remain very focused on inflation and they're more worried about the fiscal deficits here in the U.S... [as well as] the amount of Treasury supply," JoAnne Bianco, senior investment strategist at BondBloxx Investment Management, told CNBC. "All of those things make them think there needs to be more term premium." The recent spike in borrowing costs, which has seen yields move to multiyear highs, comes as the U.S. and Iran held separate talks with mediators with the aim of resolving the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, according to a report by Al Jazeera. The seven-month war continues to weigh on energy prices, fueling investor expectations of further rate hikes from the Federal Reserve to help tackle runaway price increases, which have been exacerbated by rising government debt. Traders are now pricing in a more than 72% chance of another Fed rate hike at its next meeting in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool . That comes after the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee earlier this month voted by 12-0 to raise its main interest rate by 25 basis points.

events.title: 'Threshing Day' answers questions 'Fourth Wing' fans have about Rebecca Yarros' series. Here's what you might've missed.
events.summary: "Threshing Day" is the latest book in the "Fourth Wing" universe. Casey Paul/MLB Photos via Getty Images/Red Tower Rebecca Yarros released "Threshing Day" on Tuesday. The book unveils new lore about dragons and their riders from the "Empyrean" series. It also hints at romances developing in future "Fourth Wing" books. Happy Threshing Day! OK, it's not actually Threshing Day, but Tuesday is the day Rebecca Yarros released her new "Fourth Wing" book titled "Threshing Day." No, it's not book four in the "Empyrean" series, which readers have been anxiously awaiting since "Onyx Storm" was released in 2025. It's a collection of the stories of riders from the "Fourth Wing" universe on their Threshing Days, when they bond with their dragons in their first year of training at Basgiath War College. Protagonist Violet Sorrengail doesn't have a story in the collection, as her Threshing Day appeared in "Fourth Wing." Instead, Yarros offers the perspectives of people around Violet, unveiling new lore about the riders and their dragons. The stories have major ramifications for Yarros' beloved romantasy series , including how dragons bond and hints at future romances. Here are some of the most important details you might have missed in "Threshing Day." Multiple points of view The new book includes the story of 13 Threshings, though some of those stories take place on the same day. For instance, Xaden Riorson and Garrick Tavis experience Threshing Day together, and their chapters follow the day from their respective perspectives. Notably, Yarros includes a note at the top of the book that says, "The following text has been faithfully transcribed from Navarrian into the modern language by Colonel Valin Kaori and Lieutenant Ellery Mynna, professors of Dragonkind at Basgiath War College." "Threshing Day" by Rebecca Yarros. Red Tower That note differs from those included at the start of the "Fourth Wing" novels , which are transcribed by the scribe Jesinia Neilwart. Scribes have been revealed to be unreliable narrators throughout the events of the "Empyrean" series, while Dragonkind professors have not, making "Threshing Day" more trustworthy than other books in the series. Yarros confirmed at a book release event in Denver that readers can trust the narration in "Threshing Day," unlike in the rest of her series. "It tells you that yes, this is a faithful first POV," she said. "You guys can trust what happens in this book." How Threshing works Although readers saw Violet bond her dragons, Tairn and Andarna, in "Fourth Wing," much about the actual process remained a mystery. "Threshing Day" broke down how the process works in more detail. First, several of the riders describe feeling a tugging in their chests that leads them to their dragons, as if they are calling to them. Each rider also sheds blood during Threshing. Some scratch themselves on trees or get in a fight before they bond, but in Ridoc Gamlyn's case, blood seemed to appear out of nowhere: "I note a twinge in my knee that, yep, is bleeding. Huh. I must have landed on a twig or something back there." Yarros doesn't explain why each rider bleeds during their Threshing, but dragons frequently refer to bloodlines as sources of power in the "Empyrean" series. Several of the riders also express a need or desire before bonding, which is later fulfilled by  the signet power  they develop. Brennan Sorrengail thinks to himself how important menders are moments before he bonds his dragon and goes on to become a powerful mender. Imogen Cardulo wishes she could take back something she said, and then develops the power to erase memories (more on that later). The correlation suggests that signet powers align with a rider's temperament or desires, though we'll have to see how Yarros explores that concept down the line. Rebel dragons Many of the riders featured in "Threshing Day" are children of rebels who fought against Navarre, whom readers learned in "Iron Flame" and "Onyx Storm" are secretly bonding with dragons that previously bonded with their direct family members. The practice is forbidden in Navarre because it can allow riders to develop multiple signets, creating a power imbalance. In the first chapter of "Threshing Day," Professor Colonel Thadeus Palme reveals that even the staff struggles to tell dragons apart, creating the potential for confusion. There are three novels in the "Empyrean" series to date. Red Tower "I have found that no artist has flawlessly depicted every distinguishing mark of a dragon, which makes telling descendants apart woefully difficult," he wrote. "When in doubt, it is prudent to ask a cadet for the name of their dragon." Because humans rely on riders to trace dragons, the dragons can hide their identities. For instance, Imogen bonds with Glane, who is recorded as being 19 and having never bonded with a rider before her. Yet, Imogen knows that isn't true because she met Glane as a child when she was bonded to her grandmother. Garrick's dragon also indicates he is lying about his identity, though he doesn't reveal who he is. Human lies can also enable dragons to bond with their previous riders' descendants. Xaden bonds with Sgaeyl, and in "Iron Flame," he confesses to Violet that his dragon was previously bonded to his grandfather when she discovers he has a second signet. He didn't answer Violet's questions about how that was possible in "Iron Flame," but in "Threshing Day," Yarros reveals that Xaden's public grandfather isn't his biological grandfather. His grandmother had an affair with his great-uncle, and Xaden's father was born from their affair. The public never knew Xaden's true ancestry, which allowed him to bond with Sgaeyl. Some dragons are also seeking out riders who want to overthrow Navarre and fight venin. On their Threshing Days, Xaden and Imogen tell Bodhi and Sloane Mairi that specific dragons are seeking them out because they want riders sympathetic to the rebel cause, confirming some dragons are playing an active role in the war. Venin clues As any "Fourth Wing" fan knows, "Onyx Storm" ended on a cliffhanger, with Yarros writing that an unnamed rider had joined Xaden as a venin. Garrick and Bodhi are two of the likeliest suspects, and Yarros included hints that they could have turned in "Threshing Day." Garrick repeatedly expresses a willingness to sacrifice himself for the sake of others — particularly Xaden — throughout his chapter, a practice his dragon Chradh questions. Bodhi, on the other hand, reveals that Xaden is his weakness, and he feels responsible for protecting him from abusing his power. Bodhi also worries he doesn't have an identity outside being Xaden's cousin, though bonding with his dragon Cuir seems to calm that fear. Garrick may have turned venin in the hopes of protecting others, and Bodhi could have tried to carve his own path as a venin. events.title: Trump leans on SCOTUS shadow docket more than Biden, Obama and Bush combined
events.summary: President Trump's administration on Monday filed its 41st application to the Supreme Court's shadow docket , a milestone that matches the total number of petitions it filed during his entire first term — in less than two years. Why it matters: The record highlights how often the president has turned to SCOTUS to secure authority to temporarily revive policies blocked by lower courts. What they're saying: "We have never seen an administration run to the Supreme Court with the speed and numbers that we're seeing out of the Trump administration this term," Stephen Spaulding, managing director of the Kohlberg Center at the Brennan Center for Justice, tells Axios. "Keep in mind that the shadow docket, the emergency docket, is used and should be used for actual emergencies," he says. "The administration continues to claim that they're going to face irreparable harm, and that this is an appropriate emergency for the Supreme Court to review, which we think, calls into question how the court's using the shadow docket in the first place." The other side: "President Trump has faced a historically unprecedented number of injunctions by activist lower court judges," Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, emailed Axios. "The reality is, with well over 20 Supreme Court victories the Administration's policies have been consistently upheld as lawful. President Trump will not stop implementing the America First agenda that he was elected on." How it works: The emergency, or shadow, docket lets parties seek expedited Supreme Court intervention before a case completes the ordinary appeals process. The court can, for example, pause a lower court's injunction and allow a policy to take effect while litigation continues. The orders are often issued unsigned and without explanation, complicating how lower court judges apply the orders to future cases. By the numbers: The second Trump administration filed its 41st emergency application Monday. The Biden administration made 19 requests over four years. The Obama and George W. Bush administrations made eight requests over their combined 16 years in office. Obama made three, and Bush made five. Driving the news: The 41st application asked the court to allow the Bureau of Prisons to reimplement a policy cutting off some gender-affirming care for incarcerated transgender people. U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth, a Reagan appointee, ordered the administration last month to continue providing care to people with gender dysphoria while a challenge to one of Trump's 2025 executive orders and a subsequent Bureau of Prisons policy plays out. Zoom in: Spaulding says judges' "primary tool by which they wield power" is to "explain themselves" and why they ruled a certain way. They "explain their rationale, explain their judgment, and what we've seen time and time again on the shadow docket is, in many cases, the court doesn't explain itself, and as such, is not really acting like a court." Spaulding contrasts that with lower court judges who "have taken the time to really consider the briefs. District court judges really are on the front lines of having to evaluate the claims that litigants are bringing." Zoom out: Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Elena Kagan have criticized the use of emergency docket applications to circumvent the traditional legal process. Jackson said Thursday during a law school speech that the frequent use of the shadow docket was "having an enormously disruptive and potentially corrosive effect" on the courts. Spaulding tells Axios that consistently using the docket could have "consequences for people's trust and confidence in our democracy" at a time when approval ratings of the Supreme Court are at record lows. Go deeper: Supreme Court joins Trump, Congress in job approval slump Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from the White House.

Meta uses its social networking and messaging services to gather data about users so it can use AI-powered recommender systems to present targeted ads, a service its advertiser customers find valuable. The company's online businesses (excluding virtual reality) earned $50.3 billion in profits in the first half of 2026, essentially all from advertising, and its ad revenue amounted to $114.4 billion during the same period. The company has edged toward having LLMs write those ads and also imagines AI managing some aspects of advertisers' businesses – such as responding to customer inquiries. With the new Meta Enterprise Platform, the company is now trying to capitalize on more than the fact businesses can't help but to have a presence on its social media properties. In addition to companion agents, Zuckerberg sees opportunities to sell business and coding agents, and even power customer applications through its API platform. This puts Meta in a position not only to compete with other model builders but the likes of Microsoft, Amazon, and Google – all of which have a head start in bringing AI-powered services to enterprise customers. "Initially, we will focus on bringing our full technology stack, including the Muse agent, Meta Business Agent, Muse API, Muse Code, and more to businesses and developers to help them grow," Zuckerberg wrote in a Facebook post . Leading the company's enterprise push is Chirantan "CJ" Desai, who on Monday quit as CEO of MongoDB to take the Meta gig. Desai gets the job of convincing enterprises to embrace Meta, an idea that flopped in 2016 when the company introduced Facebook At Work , a version of its social networks tuned for internal collaboration. While Meta's AI rivals – Microsoft, Amazon, and Google – have all endured various scandals, they are established B2B players and have rap sheets rather shorter than Meta's. The Social Network recently agreed to an $18 billion settlement over allegations it employed additive features that negatively affected children's health. That's just the tip of an iceberg filled with everything from perve glasses to age-inappropriate chatbots and of course the Cambridge Analytica scandal . events.title: Battery customers feeling 'ripped off' after solar company collapses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Macarthur Solar customers furious and without batteries after company collapses Murray Wylie paid a $5,000 deposit for a solar battery system that he never received. ( ABC News: Chris Taylor ) A Sydney solar company has collapsed, leaving large numbers of customers furious after they paid hefty deposits for battery systems under a multi-billion-dollar federal government scheme. The ABC previously revealed allegations of rorting and misconduct under the same scheme. Consumer advocates are calling for an urgent increase to protections, oversight and regulation. Murray Wylie was fed up after shelling out a $5,000 deposit for a solar battery system in February, which Macarthur Solar had still not installed by August. The company kept reassuring him, but Mr Wylie had doubts. In late August he drove to Macarthur's south-west Sydney office. But on arrival he was confronted by locked doors and a deserted office. "I was angry because the thoughts that were building up had come true. I wasn't going to get my battery," he said. "You feel like you're being ripped off." When Murray Wylie questioned why the solar battery installation was taking so long Macarthur Solar told him to be patient. ( ABC News: Chris Taylor ) Macarthur Solar's underlying company, Macarthur Energy, had gone bust. Mathew Cox, a local electrician, founded it in 2015. The ABC spoke to eight Macarthur customers who fear they lost large deposits for solar and battery installations that never arrived, ranging from $1,500 to $17,600. Many signed up with Macarthur Solar after being attracted by a generous federal government subsidy, the Cheaper Home Batteries Program (CHBP). The program sparked unprecedented demand, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025 at an estimated cost of more than $7.2 billion over four years. Macarthur's customers were charged 50 per cent up-front, far above what's considered industry standard. NSW home building laws limit deposits to 10 per cent and leading solar and consumer advocates say the higher deposits may have breached those laws. The state's Building Commission confirmed it was investigating after receiving more than 100 complaints. Macarthur Energy owes almost $3.4 million to more than 79 unsecured creditors, including former customers and suppliers, according to a report by liquidator Daniel Soire of Jones Partners. Sixteen former employees are also seriously out of pocket, owed more than $420,000 for superannuation, annual leave and redundancy payments. Consumer and solar advocates say Macarthur Solar's collapse highlights glaring holes in protections. "The current system is absolutely failing consumers," said Andy Kelly, Choice's director of consumer impact. Mr Wylie had rooftop panels but contacted Macarthur because he was thinking about adding a battery. They came to his house for a consultation. "They seemed fair dinkum," he said. When Mr Wylie checked in at the office about when his installation would happen, he was told to be patient. In June, the company changed the battery he would get. Eventually, he was told it would be installed at the end of August, but that never happened. Mark Barnes is out of pocket $6,500 after signing a contract with Macarthur Solar. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) Mark Barnes paid a $6,500 deposit that he fears he will not get back. "We signed a contract in good faith and got nothing," he said. Mr Barnes has now paid another installer for solar panels and a battery system, meaning he has paid twice. The loss means the retiree, who is on a part-pension, has been left with less money to spend on his grandkids. Mr Barnes handed his money over in December. However, he claims the company was repeatedly "stalling". In May, he called the battery system's supplier for help, which prompted a call from the owner, Mathew Cox, and eventually led to a commitment to install the system in July. Despite assurances from the owner of Macarthur Solar that his system would be installed, Mark Barnes says no work has been completed at his property. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) That came and went, so he chased Mr Cox, but says he stopped responding. Mr Barnes demanded a refund and lodged a complaint with the New South Wales Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT), the state's small claims tribunal, however the company went into liquidation before his case was finalised. The ABC has seen three NCAT and court orders secured by other customers against Macarthur Energy ordering repayment for amounts between $1,600 and $17,600.

events.title: 10 years on, Geelong and Broadmeadows count the cost of Ford's departure
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Geelong and Broadmeadows economies back on track a decade after Ford closures Anthony Anderson, Tony Travers and Henry Fuller spent many years building Ford vehicles. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) He worked at Ford for 28 years and still proudly wears a jacket with the big blue logo. He is also one of 17 in his family who worked at Geelong's Ford factory across its 90-year history. For him, the decade since it closed has been difficult. Former Ford workers Tony Travers, Henry Fuller and Anthony Anderson. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) It's hard to sum up how important the factory was to Geelong. Mr Travers describes the suburb of Norlane as the town Ford built, full of factory workers and their families. During World War II, the plant manufactured long-range fuel tanks for aircraft. When the war ended, it moulded or stamped together large metal sheets into car panels and created the company's well-known straight-six engines. The plant became a microcosm of Australian multiculturalism, drawing postwar migrants to Geelong for the consistent work. Parts for cars including the Falcon, Fairlane and Territory were made in the sprawling Norlane complex and taken to Broadmeadows, where workers welded the panels together, painted the shells and inserted the Geelong-built engines. The final car rolled off the production line at Broadmeadows in 2016. ( Supplied: Ford Australia ) Ford said both factories employed about 5,000 people in its heyday. But that all changed in 2013, when management announced it would close the plants. The American car maker initially announced about 1,200 manufacturing jobs would become redundant at both sites. When the doors closed on October 7, 2016 , many workers had already moved on or been redeployed. The writing had been on the wall for years. In 2013, Ford president Bob Graziano said the company lost more than $600 million over five years on its Australian operations and its costs were "double that of Europe and nearly four times Ford in Asia". Mr Travers was selected to stay on at the factory, working on prototypes, until 2017. When he finished, he found a variety of short-term work, building camper trailers, filling potholes and replacing traffic signs. But he says none of it was as good as his time at Ford. Tony Travers worked at both the Geelong and Broadmeadows factories. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) "You knew your job every day. When I transitioned to these other places, they did things completely differently, and it made it extremely difficult … you had to get your mind out of the Ford way of doing things," he said. Now retired, he remembers the satisfaction of creating such useful products. The closure was such a seismic shift for many of the 600 workers who finished 10 years ago, their bosses gave them a strategy to deal with the disruption to their routine after the closures. "They said on Monday morning just drive into the work car park as per normal, park your car, sit there for a few minutes, and then drive home," Mr Travers said. It touches on a wider feeling among former Ford workers, who talk about being part of a Ford family, in clearly defined jobs. "You're almost institutionalised," says Mr Travers's former colleague, Henry Fuller, who worked at Ford Geelong for 35 years. Henry Fuller has driven buses for most of the past 10 years and is now looking for part-time work. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) Mr Fuller remembers 2013 to 2016 as tough. In the final days of the Geelong factory, part of Anthony Anderson's job was to help his colleagues find other work. He found the mock interviews the hardest part. "People just hadn't done an interview for, say, 25 years. To get them writing resumes and having the confidence to go and present themselves to a new employer wasn't easy," he said. Anthony Anderson worked at Ford Geelong for 33 years. ( ABC News: Jonathon Kendall ) Mr Anderson agrees many had worked with Ford for so long they felt institutionalised. "When you finish, you will not find the same wages and conditions or the attitude that's on the shop floor here. "You won't necessarily find a comfortable job first off. You may go through four or five jobs," he said. He told many to take time off after the closure, advice he took himself, before he became secretary and treasurer of the Geelong Trades Hall Council. While Ford stopped making cars in Australia, it said it employed about 1,000 people at a research facility in Geelong, testing grounds in the You Yangs, and its Campbellfield site. After the closure, Geelong's unemployment rate was 6.5 per cent. It has now improved to 4.5 per cent.

events.title: Homeowners are sitting on record equity – and not using it
events.summary: U.S. homeowners have more housing wealth than ever before, thanks to fast-rising home prices over the last several years -- but they aren't spending much of it. In the second quarter of this year, there was a collective $11.5 trillion in so-called "tappable" home equity, according to Cotality, a data technology company. "The borrowers with the most housing wealth are often the least likely to tap it," said Thom Malone, principal economist at Cotality. "They tend to have low mortgage rates, strong cash flow, and little reason to move." A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. U.S. homeowners have more housing wealth than ever before, thanks to fast-rising home prices over the last several years. But they aren't spending very much of it. In the second quarter of this year, there was a collective $11.5 trillion in so-called "tappable" home equity, according to Cotality, a data technology company. That is the amount borrowers could take out in debt while still leaving enough in the home to satisfy lenders. In total equity, borrowers with a mortgage have $17.9 trillion, or, on average, $310,000 per homeowner, which is $6,000 more than they had in the previous three months. While homeowners did originate nearly 20% more second mortgages or home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) compared with the first quarter, it still represented less than 0.1% of the total tappable equity that they could have used. Get Property Play directly to your inbox CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox. So all that cash sits on the sidelines and continues to compound because home prices in most areas of the country are still seeing small gains. Consumers are also increasingly nervous about the state of the economy and rising interest rates. Taking out a second loan would mean doing so at a much higher rate than they likely have on their primary mortgage, which most people won't do unless absolutely necessary. Mortgage rates dropped to record lows in the first two years of the Covid pandemic, meaning anyone who purchased a home during or before that time has a rate that is at least one third of what rates are today. Those lower monthly payments give them much stronger cash flow in general, so they're able to fund things like renovations or even college tuition without digging into their home equity. All real estate is local, and there are wide variations as equity is heaviest in the West and Northeast. Average homeowner equity levels in Hawaii and California were over $600,000 and over $400,000 in Massachusetts. In Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Iowa, by contrast, equity levels are just over $100,000. Not only are the differences stark but they are actually widening, as home price appreciation is stronger in already high-equity markets. While homeowners in most states have gained equity, some are seeing home values drop and are therefore losing equity. These include states like Texas, Minnesota, Colorado, and Maryland, as well as the District of Columbia. The share of borrowers who owe more on their mortgages than their homes are worth, so-called underwater mortgages, is still quite low at just 2.1%.

events.title: Trump government ads were funded by Homeland Security, WSJ reports
events.summary: U.S. Customs and Border Protection funded the taxpayer-backed television ads featuring President Donald Trump that have drawn bipartisan scrutiny ahead of the midterm election, The Wall Street Journal reported. Top congressional Democrats say the administration dedicated $20 million to the effort, including funds provided to CBP through Republicans’ “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” Trump personally pushed for the ads and was involved in their creation, according to the Journal, as lawmakers question whether taxpayer funds were improperly used for political messaging. Taxpayer money from U.S. Customs and Border Protection funded the pro-Trump television ads that have drawn bipartisan scrutiny just weeks before November's midterm election , The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday. President Donald Trump personally pushed for the ads and was involved in creating them, the Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The revelation puts a CBP, part of the Department of Homeland Security, behind a campaign that looks far different from its traditional public messaging. CBP routinely runs ads discouraging illegal immigration. These spots instead feature Trump heavily, tout his tax cuts , attack communism and recycle language from his 2024 campaign. One ad declares that "America will never be a communist country" as images of Trump fill the screen. Another revives his "final battle" message from the 2024 race and attacks the political establishment and news media. The ads have already aired thousands of times nationally and locally. CNBC previously reported that more than $1.2 million had been spent airing two of the spots, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising spending. Democrats and at least one Republican senator have questioned whether taxpayer dollars should be used for ads centered so heavily on Trump. Some Democrats in Congress are now calling for investigations into whether money appropriated for border protection is being used to promote the president's political message. "It appears DHS has dedicated $20 million to this outrageous scheme," Sens. Patty Murray , D-Wash., and Chris Murphy , D-Conn., wrote in a letter to DHS on Tuesday, saying the department tapped money provided to CBP through Republicans' " One Big Beautiful Bill Act ." Federal contracting records show CBP awarded $20 million to Maryland-based advertising firm LMD Agency on Sept. 20 for a "National Media Campaign." The one-year contract was fully funded at the time of the award. The award came one day after the Office of Management and Budget approved the release of $20 million to CBP under a "Commemorative Events" funding line. The public contract record does not specify what the "National Media Campaign" entails or establish that LMD worked on the Trump ads. LMD has previously performed advertising work for agencies within the Department of Homeland Security, federal procurement records show. LMD did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on whether its $20 million contract is connected to the ads, whether it is playing a role in the ad campaign or whether additional advertisements or media buys are planned. CBP did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the ads or the procurement contract. Blowback to the ads also spread to federal regulators Tuesday. Watchdog group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the Federal Communications Commission and Federal Trade Commission urging broadcasters to stop airing the ads, while separately asking the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel last Friday to investigate alleged violations of federal propaganda restrictions and the Hatch Act, which restricts the involvement of federal government employees in political campaigns. The White House defended the campaign Tuesday, calling the spots public service announcements. “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson told CNBC. “The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country.”

events.title: Soho House venue under investigation for food safety
events.summary: Shoreditch House is one of 10 Soho House locations in London A venue of private members club Soho House is being investigated by the local council after a former member of staff raised concerns about rats and out-of-date food allegedly being served. The former staff member told BBC News he was pressured to replace labels on prepared food if it was not sold at the end of the day and said he regularly saw rats at the venue. His contract was terminated two months after he first raised concerns, but Soho House said this was unrelated to his complaints. It added that the food incident was isolated and re-labelling unsold food was not company policy. Hackney Council has confirmed it is investigating food safety and hygiene at Soho House's Shoreditch location. Soho House is a popular haunt for A-list celebrities. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle reportedly had their first date at one of its London venues. The former staff member at Shoreditch House, Kamran Khan, first raised concerns informally about the alleged re-labelling practice before formally filing a complaint with Soho House. Khan was on probation at the venue when he raised the concerns in July, and his employment was terminated earlier in September. Following his formal complaint, the company investigated and told Khan on 24 August there was evidence to support his claim and steps were being taken to address the matter. Khan claimed the practice continued despite the assurances he was allegedly offered, leading him to complain to Hackney Council instead. A spokesperson for the council said: "We have received a report about food safety and hygiene at Shoreditch House and have opened an investigation." Speaking to BBC News, Khan said he was told in a probation meeting to continue the practice. The 30-year-old, who told BBC News he has had several jobs in catering and hospitality said he was told "if I don't change labels on my own initiative, [they] would take that as a performance concern". He said he felt compelled to raise the issue because he saw a lot of children and pregnant women at the restaurant. "I told them that I don't want to be held personally liable for anyone that gets injured," he said. Food served in a restaurant must legally be labelled with information including the best-before or use-by date. Khan also said there had been rats at the venue for a long time and that cleaners were told to check daily for rat droppings. A spokesperson for Soho House said: "We're really sorry that this isolated food labelling incident took place at one of our kitchens. This is not how we expect our houses to operate and it is not company policy." They said an external, independent investigation and audit was conducted. "Delivering the highest level of food safety for our members and guests is incredibly important to us," they added. "For clarity, the former employee's contract was terminated for reasons entirely unrelated to food labelling." Soho House membership starts from £291.67 monthly or £204.17 for under-27s. The group opened its first club in London in 1995, and now has 46 Soho Houses in Europe, North America and Asia, as well a string of other up-market hospitality businesses. The company listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021, but its share price dropped sharply in the following years as it struggled to make a profit and fought accusations it was losing its exclusivity. It was bought by a consortium of investors last year , with actor Ashton Kutcher joining the company's board. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters SPONSORED POST: How agentic AI, real-time visibility, and stronger governance can help enterprises protect critical services and manage increasingly complex IT environments. When a critical application fails, the last thing an IT team needs is a debate over who's responsible. Yet in complex enterprise environments, network, application, and compute teams often rely on separate legacy monitoring tools, each providing only part of the picture. Identifying the root cause can become a time-consuming exercise while essential services remain unavailable. As organizations expand their use of AI, hybrid infrastructure, and sovereign cloud environments, the challenge is becoming more pressing. The systems supporting critical services are growing more interconnected, while the need for resilience, operational efficiency, and effective governance continues to increase. AI agents are starting to take on some of that operational load, but an agent reasoning from legacy monitoring data sees the same partial picture the humans do. But are enterprise leaders seeing the same risks as the teams responsible for keeping these systems running? Research by Virtana suggests a significant observability gap between what boardrooms believe they know about their IT environments and what frontline operators experience. In this interview, The Register's Tim Phillips speaks with Paul Appleby, CEO of Virtana, about the limitations of legacy monitoring approaches and how agentic observability could help organizations gain a clearer picture of their infrastructure. Appleby explores why fragmented legacy monitoring can leave IT teams struggling to distinguish the cause of an incident from its symptoms, and how agentic observability, which correlates real-time telemetry across applications, cloud, infrastructure, networks, and AI systems, gives AI agents the context to accelerate root cause analysis and remediation. The discussion also examines the growing importance of observability for data sovereignty and AI infrastructure. As enterprises invest in AI factories and increasingly complex workloads, Appleby considers how organizations can maintain visibility across the technology stack, strengthen governance, and address operational risks before they disrupt critical services. For IT leaders, the interview offers a perspective on moving beyond the traditional focus on proving which team wasn't responsible, toward faster resolution, preventative observability, and more resilient operations. It also raises an important question for executive teams: Is investment in governance and operational controls keeping pace with the infrastructure and AI services their businesses increasingly depend on?
